가.etymology: Native Korean nominative (subject) case particle attached to vowel-final nouns, first attested in early Modern Korean (16th–17th centuries) as a phonological complement to older 이.
가.notes: Pairs allomorphically with 이 after consonant-final nouns.

가게.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가게 ('temporary market stall or awning added onto a building').
가게.notes: Everyday native word for a small retail shop, alongside Sino-Korean 상점 (商店).

가격.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 가격 (價格), joining 가 (價, 'price, value') and 격 (格, 'standard, level').
가격.notes: Coexists with native Korean 값 ('price, worth', as in 반값 'half price').

가구.etymology: Sino-Korean 가구 (家具), compounding 가 (家, 'house, home') and 구 (具, 'utensil, implement, furnishing').

가까이.etymology: Native Korean derived adverb and noun formed from the stem 가깝- of 가깝다 ('to be near, close', Middle Korean 갓갑다) + adverbial/nominalizing suffix -이.

가끔.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'sometimes, from time to time', attested in Early Modern Korean as 갓금 / 가끔, likely related to 갈다 ('to alternate') or 금 ('dividing line, interval').

가느다랗다.etymology: Native Korean adjective built from the stem 가늘- of 가늘다 ('to be thin, slender', Middle Korean 가늘다) + expressive intensive suffix -다랗다.

가다.etymology: Core native Korean verb of motion descending directly from Middle Korean 가다 ('to go, move away, pass').
가다.notes: Also serves as a productive directional and aspectual auxiliary verb (-어 가다).

가득.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 가득 ('full to the brim, abundantly').
가득.notes: Combines with 하다 to form 가득하다 ('to be full') and pairs with 차다 ('to fill up').

가디건.etymology: Borrowed from English cardigan (named after James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan), referring to an open-front knitted sweater.
가디건.notes: Prescriptive orthography lists 카디건, while 가디건 is widespread in everyday usage.

가르치다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 가르치다 ('to teach, instruct; to point out'), historically derived from the root of 가르다 ('to divide, discern').
가르치다.notes: In Modern Korean, the older single verb split into 가르치다 ('to teach') and 가리키다 ('to point at').

가리키다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to point at, indicate', diverging in Early Modern Korean from Middle Korean 가르치다 ('to point out; to teach').

가만히.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from the root 가만 (Middle Korean 가만, 'quietly, still') + adverbial suffix -히.

가방.etymology: Entered Korean in the late 19th–early 20th century via Japanese 鞄 (kaban, 'bag, satchel'), itself widely traced to Dutch kabas ('handbag, basket') or Chinese 夾板.
가방.notes: Functions like a core everyday noun covering backpacks, briefcases, and travel suitcases.

가볍다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 가챦다 (> 가볍다, 'light in weight, not heavy').

가스레인지.etymology: Loanword compound from English gas range, combining gas ('fuel gas') and range ('cooking stove').

가슴.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가숌 ('chest, breast, heart').

가운데.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가온대, a compound of 가온 ('middle, center') and 대 ('place, spot').

가을.etymology: Native Korean season noun descending from Middle Korean 가싦 ('autumn, harvest season').

가이드북.etymology: Borrowed from English guidebook (guide + book), referring to a printed handbook for travellers or visitors.

가장.etymology: Native Korean superlative adverb descending from Middle Korean 가장 ('to the utmost limit; most').

가져가다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound joining 가지다 ('to have, hold, take') + connective -어 + 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to take away, carry with one

가져다드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble compound verb formed from 가져다 (contracted from 가지어다가, 'take and shift location') + 드리다 (humble verb 'to give').

history.meaning: to bring and present to an elder/superior

가져다주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 가져다 (contracted from 가지어다가, 'take and transfer') + 주다 ('to give').

history.meaning: to bring and give to someone

가져오다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound joining 가지다 ('to hold, take') + connective -어 + 오다 ('to come').

가족.etymology: Sino-Korean 가족 (家族), compounding 가 (家, 'house, household') and 족 (族, 'clan, kin, lineage').

가족분.etymology: Hybrid honorific compound combining Sino-Korean 가족 (家族, 'family') with the native Korean honorific person suffix/classifier -분 ('esteemed person').

가죽.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가짗 ('skin, hide, leather'), derived from 갗 ('skin') + suffix -욱.

가지.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가지 ('tree branch; kind, sort, variety').
가지.notes: The sense 'kind, category' developed metaphorically from branches ramifying from a single trunk.

가지다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 가지다 ('to hold in hand, possess, keep').
가지다.notes: Frequently contracted in speech and writing to 갖다.

가판대.etymology: Sino-Korean 가판대 (街販臺), from 가 (街, 'street') + 판 (販, 'sell, trade') + 대 (臺, 'platform, stand').

간단하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 간단 (簡單, 간 'bamboo slip, brief, simple' + 단 'single, uncomplicated') + native adjective-forming verb -하다.

간지럽다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective from Middle Korean 간지랍다, built on the sensory root 간질- ('tickling sensation') + adjective-forming suffix -업다.

간판.etymology: Sino-Korean 간판 (看板), combining 간 (看, 'look at, view') and 판 (板, 'wooden board, plank').

갈다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 갈다 ('to grind, whet, sharpen; to plow; to replace/change').

갈라지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 갈라- (infinitive stem of 가르다, 'to divide, split') + inchoative auxiliary -지다 ('to become').

갈색.etymology: Sino-Korean 갈색 (褐色), compounding 갈 (褐, 'coarse undyed hempen/woollen cloth, brown') and 색 (色, 'color').

갈수록.etymology: Lexicalized native Korean adverb formed from the stem 가- of 가다 ('to go, progress') + correlative ending -ㄹ수록 ('the more ... the more').

갈아입다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 갈아- (from 갈다, 'to change, replace') and 입다 ('to put on, wear clothes').

감다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 감다, representing homophonous roots meaning 'to close (one's eyes)', 'to wind/coil around', and 'to wash (hair)/bathe'.

history.meaning: to close (eyes); to wind/wrap; to bathe
to close (eyes); to wind/coil; to wash (hair)

감독하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 감독 (監督, 감 'inspect, watch over' + 독 'oversee, direct') + verbalizer -하다.
감독하다.notes: Used for overseeing a workplace, directing a film, or coaching a team.

감사하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 감사 (感謝, 감 'feel, be moved' + 사 'thank, express gratitude') + native verb/adjective suffix -하다.

감사합니다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 감사 (感謝, 'gratitude, appreciation') plus the formal polite form 합니다 of 하다 ('to do').
감사합니다.notes: Alongside native Korean 고맙습니다 / 고마워요, this is the everyday standard way to thank someone politely.

감상적.etymology: Sino-Korean 감상적 (感傷的), from 감상 (感傷, 감 'feel' + 상 'grieve, wound', 'sentimentality') + determiner suffix -적 (的).

감싸다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 감- (from 감다, 'to wind around, coil') and 싸다 ('to wrap, cover').

갓.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'just now, freshly, newly', attested in Early Modern Korean as 갓 and historically related to Middle Korean 갓/가장 ('just, barely').

history.meaning: freshly, just (e.g. 갓 구운 빵 'freshly baked bread')

강.etymology: Sino-Korean 강 (江, 'river'), from Middle Chinese *kæwng (originally the proper name of the Yangtze River, generalized to large rivers).
강.notes: Replaced older native Korean 가람 ('river') in everyday vocabulary.

강물.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 강 (江, 'river') with native Korean 물 ('water').

강철.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 강철 (鋼鐵), from 강 (鋼, 'tempered steel') and 철 (鐵, 'iron').
강철.notes: Literally 'hardened iron', used for high-tension piano wire and hardware.

같다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 갋다 ('to be like, be the same as').

history.meaning: to be the same, like, similar

같이.etymology: Native Korean adverb and postposition from Middle Korean 가티, derived from the stem 갋- of 같다 ('to be the same') + adverbial suffix -이.
같이.notes: Pronounced [가치] via regular palatalization of ㅌ before ㅣ.

개.etymology: Represents both the Sino-Korean bound counter 개 (個, 'individual item, piece') and the native Korean noun 개 ('dog', from Middle Korean 가히).

개방.etymology: Sino-Korean 개방 (開放), compounding 개 (開, 'open') and 방 (放, 'release, let out').

개방하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 개방 (開放, 'opening up') + native light verb -하다 ('to do').

개업.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 개업 (開業), from 개 (開, 'open, begin') and 업 (業, 'business, trade').
개업.notes: Refers to launching a new shop, café, or practice.

개인.etymology: Sino-Korean 개인 (個人), compounding 개 (個, 'single, individual') and 인 (人, 'person').

개짜리.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the Sino-Korean unit counter 개 (個, 'piece, item') with the native suffix -짜리 ('worth of, consisting of that number of units').

거.etymology: Colloquial native Korean bound noun contracted from 것 ('thing, object, fact', Middle Korean 것) by dropping final -ㅅ.

거기.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative place pronoun descending from Middle Korean 그어긔, contracted from 그 ('that, near listener') + 어긔 ('place').

거리.etymology: Represents both native Korean 거리 ('street, road, thoroughfare'; also 'material/stuff for', from Middle Korean 거리) and Sino-Korean 거리 (距離, 거 'distance' + 리 'separate', 'distance').

거스름돈.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 거스름 (deverbal noun from 거스르다, 'to go counter to, return change') and 돈 ('money').

거울.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 거우로 ('mirror, looking glass').

걱정.etymology: Korean noun first attested in Early Modern Korean (17th century) as 걱졍 ('worry, anxiety, concern'), of native or obscured origin.

걱정하다.etymology: Formed from 걱정 ('worry, concern') + native verb-forming suffix -하다.

건너.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb derived from the stem of 건너다 (Middle Korean 건너다, 'to cross over to the other side').

건너가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 건너- (from 건너다, 'to cross') and 가다 ('to go').

건너다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 건너다 ('to cross a river, road, or boundary').

건너편.etymology: Hybrid compound combining native 건너 ('across, opposite') with Sino-Korean 편 (便, 'side, direction').

history.meaning: the opposite side, across the way

건네주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 건네- (from 건네다, causative of 건너다, 'to pass across, hand over') and 주다 ('to give').

history.meaning: to hand over, pass to someone

건물.etymology: Sino-Korean 건물 (建物), compounding 건 (建, 'build, erect') and 물 (物, 'thing, structure').

건물주.etymology: Sino-Korean 건물주 (建物主), formed from 건물 (建物, 'building') + 주 (主, 'owner, proprietor').

건반.etymology: Sino-Korean 鍵盤 'keyboard': the board of keys on a piano or similar instrument.
건반.notes: A piano key is never 열쇠, the word for a door key.

건반투성이.etymology: Hybrid compound joining Sino-Korean 건반 (鍵盤, 건 'key' + 반 'board', 'musical keyboard') and native suffix -투성이 ('covered with, full of').

history.meaning: full of keys / covered in keyboard keys

건축.etymology: Sino-Korean 건축 (建築), compounding 건 (建, 'establish, erect') and 축 (築, 'build, construct').

건축가.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character noun 건축가 (建築家): 건축 ('architecture, building') + specialist suffix -가 (家, 'expert, professional').
건축가.notes: The same suffix -가 appears in 작가 (作家, 'writer, author').

건축법.etymology: Sino-Korean 건축법 (建築法), combining 건축 (建築, 'architecture, building construction') and 법 (法, 'law, act, code').

걷다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 걷다 ('to walk', ㄷ-irregular: 걸어) or homophonous 걷다 ('to roll up sleeves, fold back, gather', regular: 걷어).

history.meaning: to walk; to roll up, gather
to walk; to roll up / collect

걸다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 걸다 ('to hang, hook, fasten, stake').

history.meaning: to hang, latch, dial/speak to (말을 걸다)

걸리다.etymology: Native Korean passive and intransitive verb derived from 걸다 ('to hang, hook') + passive suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to be hung, get caught, take (time)

걸쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from the verb stem 걸- of 걸다 ('to hook, fasten') and 쇠 ('iron, metal').

걸어가다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound from 걸어- (infinitive of 걷다, 'to walk') + 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to walk (to a place), go on foot

걸어오다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound from 걸어- (infinitive of 걷다, 'to walk') + 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to walk here, come on foot

걸음.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun descending from Middle Korean 거름, formed from 걷-/걸- ('to walk') + nominalizing suffix -음.

검다.etymology: Native Korean basic color adjective descending from Middle Korean 검다 ('to be black, dark').

겁쟁이.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound joining Sino-Korean 겁 (怯, 'fear, timidity') with the native characterizing person suffix -쟁이.

것.etymology: Native Korean bound noun attested in Middle Korean as 것 ('thing, object, fact'). In everyday spoken Korean it regularly contracts to 거, with subject 게, topic 건, and object 걸.
것.notes: Essential building block in grammar patterns such as -(으)ㄹ 거예요 ('will') and -(으)ㄴ 것 같아요 ('seems like').

겉면.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 겉 ('outer surface, exterior', Middle Korean 것) with Sino-Korean 면 (面, 'face, surface').
겉면.notes: Pronounced [건면] by nasal assimilation of 겉 [걷] before ㅁ.

게다가.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 거기에다가 (거기 'there' + locative-additive -에다가 'in addition to').

게스트하우스.etymology: Borrowed from English guesthouse (guest + house), denoting a small lodging house or traveller's inn.

겨울.etymology: Native Korean season noun descending from Middle Korean 겨싦 ('winter').

격자틀.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 격자 (格子, 격 'grid, lattice' + 자 'object') with native 틀 ('frame, framework').

결국.etymology: Sino-Korean 결국 (結局), compounding 결 (結, 'tie up, conclude') and 국 (局, 'board game match, situation'); originally referred to finishing a game of Go (바둑).

history.meaning: conclusion of a game or affair
in the end, ultimately, after all

결정.etymology: Sino-Korean 결정 (決定), compounding 결 (決, 'decide, breach a dike') and 정 (定, 'settle, fix').
결정.notes: Combines with 하다 ('decide') or 내리다 ('make/hand down a decision').

겹치다.etymology: Native Korean verb derived from 겹 (Middle Korean 겹, 'layer, fold, ply') + verbalizing/intensive suffix -치다.

경첩.etymology: Korean hardware noun attested in Early Modern Korean as 경쳡, referring to the two folding metal leaves that join a door or lid to its frame.

계단.etymology: Sino-Korean 계단 (階段), compounding 계 (階, 'steps, stairs, rank') and 단 (段, 'step, stage, tier').

계단참.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 계단 (階段, 'stairs') with native 참 ('resting station, stage along a route').

계란.etymology: Sino-Korean 계란 (鷄卵), compounding 계 (鷄, 'chicken, domestic fowl') and 란 (卵, 'egg').
계란.notes: Used interchangeably in everyday Korean with native 달걀.

계산.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 계산 (計算), from 계 (計, 'measure, plan, sum up') and 산 (算, 'reckon, count').
계산.notes: In shops and cafés, 계산하다 is the everyday verb for settling the bill at the register.

계산하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 계산 (計算, 계 'count, reckon' + 산 'calculate with counting rods') + native light verb -하다.

history.meaning: to calculate; to settle/pay a bill

계속.etymology: Sino-Korean 계속 (繼續), compounding 계 (繼, 'succeed, carry on') and 속 (續, 'connect, continue').

계시다.etymology: Native Korean subject-honorific existential verb descending from Middle Korean 겨시다 ('to be, stay, dwell [honorific]').

계약.etymology: Sino-Korean 계약 (契約), compounding 계 (契, 'engraved tally, deed, covenant') and 약 (約, 'bind, promise, agreement').

계약과.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 계약 (契約, 'contract') + either Sino-Korean suffix -과 (課, 'department, division') or native comitative particle -과 ('and/with').

history.meaning: contracts division (契約課) / with the contract (계약+과)

계약서.etymology: Sino-Korean 계약서 (契約書), combining 계약 (契約, 'contract, agreement') and 서 (書, 'written document').

계피.etymology: Sino-Korean 계피 (桂皮), compounding 계 (桂, 'cassia / cinnamon tree') and 피 (皮, 'bark, skin').

history.meaning: dried bark of the cassia tree

계획.etymology: Sino-Korean 계획 (計劃), compounding 계 (計, 'reckon, calculate') and 획 (劃, 'draw lines, lay out, devise').

계획하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 계획 (計劃, 'plan, project') + native light verb -하다.

고개.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 고개 ('mountain ridge or pass; nape of the neck, head').

history.meaning: mountain pass; back of the neck, head

고개.notes: The anatomical sense ('head/neck' in 고개를 끄덕이다 'nod one's head') and topographical sense ('hill crest') share the image of a curved crest.

고르다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 고르다 ('to make even or uniform; to sort out, select').

고맙다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 고맙다 ('worthy of reverence, grateful'), related to an older root associated with respect.
고맙다.notes: Conjugates as a ㅂ-irregular adjective: 고마워요 in polite speech and 고맙습니다 in formal speech.

고모.etymology: Sino-Korean 고모 (姑母), compounding 고 (姑, 'father's sister') and 모 (母, 'mother, older female relative').
고모.notes: Distinguished in Korean kinship from 이모 (姨母, mother's sister) and 숙모 (叔母, father's brother's wife).

고모님.etymology: Hybrid honorific kinship term combining Sino-Korean 고모 (姑母, 'paternal aunt') with the native honorific suffix -님.

고장.etymology: Represents both Sino-Korean 고장 (故障, 고 'incident' + 장 'obstruction', meaning 'mechanical breakdown, malfunction') and native Korean 고장 (Middle Korean 곳양, 'region, locality, hometown').

고정하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 고정 (固定, 고 'firm, solid' + 정 'fix in place') + -하다.
고정하다.notes: Standard carpentry and mechanical verb for fastening panels, screws, or hinges.

고집.etymology: Sino-Korean 고집 (固執), compounding 고 (固, 'firm, solid, obstinate') and 집 (執, 'grasp, hold fast').

고치다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 고티다 ('to mend, repair, alter, cure'), with regular palatalization of 티 > 치.

곡.etymology: Sino-Korean 곡 (曲, 'melody, tune, musical piece; bend'), from Middle Chinese *khjowk.

history.meaning: piece of music, song, tune (also counter for songs)

곧.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 곧 ('on the spot, immediately, soon, namely').

골목.etymology: Native Korean compound noun joining 골 (Middle Korean 골, 'valley, narrow lane between houses') and 목 ('neck, narrow passage').

곱다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 곱다 ('to be fine, lovely, delicate, smooth').
곱다.notes: Conjugates as 고와 / 고운; describes both refined beauty and finely ground powder or sand.

곳.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 곳 ('place, spot, locality').

공간.etymology: Sino-Korean 공간 (空間), compounding 공 (空, 'empty, sky, void') and 간 (間, 'interval, room, space between').

공구함.etymology: Sino-Korean 공구함 (工具函), combining 공구 (工具, 공 'work, craft' + 구 'tool') and 함 (函, 'box, case').

공기.etymology: Sino-Korean 공기 (空氣), compounding 공 (空, 'sky, empty space') and 기 (氣, 'vapor, breath, atmosphere').

공손하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 공손 (恭遜, 공 'reverent, respectful' + 손 'humble, deferential') + native adjective-forming verb -하다.

공식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 공식 (公式), from 공 (公, 'public, official') and 식 (式, 'form, ceremony, formula').

공연장.etymology: Sino-Korean 공연장 (公演場), from 공연 (公演, 공 'public' + 연 'perform') + 장 (場, 'place, hall, venue').

공짜.etymology: Sino-Korean 공 (空) 'empty' with the native suffix -짜: something that costs nothing.
공짜.notes: Casual; 공짜로 means 'for free'. The same suffix appears in 진짜 'the real thing' and 가짜 'a fake'.

과장님.etymology: Hybrid honorific title combining Sino-Korean 과장 (課長, 과 'section, department' + 장 'head, chief') with the native honorific suffix -님.

관리.etymology: Sino-Korean 관리 (管理), compounding 관 (管, 'pipe, key, oversee, control') and 리 (理, 'put in order, administer').

광장.etymology: Sino-Korean 광장 (廣場), compounding 광 (廣, 'wide, broad, spacious') and 장 (場, 'open ground, place').

괜찮다.etymology: Contracted in Early Modern Korean from 관계하지 아니하다 (Sino-Korean 관계 關係 'relation, concern' + negated -하지 아니하다 'does not matter'), via 괜치 않다 > 괜찮다.

history.meaning: to not matter, be of no concern
to be okay, fine, all right, decent

교회.etymology: Sino-Korean 교회 (敎會), compounding 교 (敎, 'teaching, religion') and 회 (會, 'assembly, gathering').

history.meaning: church (especially Protestant church in contemporary South Korea)

구.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 구 (九, 'nine'), from Middle Chinese *kjuwX; also used for Sino-Korean 구 (區, 'district, ward').

구도심.etymology: Sino-Korean 구도심 (舊都心), combining prefix 구- (舊, 'old, former') with 도심 (都心, 도 'capital, metropolis' + 심 'heart, center').

구두.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from Japanese kutsu (靴, 'shoes'; voiced to -gutsu in compounds), referring in Korean specifically to Western-style or dress shoes.
구두.notes: Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 구두 (口頭, 'oral, verbal', as in 구두 계약 'verbal agreement').

구리.etymology: Native Korean metal noun descending from Middle Korean 구리 ('copper, bronze').

구멍.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 구무 / 구멍 ('hole, opening, cavity').

구석.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 구석 ('inner corner, nook, recessed spot').

구하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 구 (求, 'seek, request, obtain', or 救, 'save, rescue') + native verb-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to look for, get, find; to save/rescue

구호실.etymology: Sino-Korean 구호실 (救護室), combining 구호 (救護, 구 'rescue, relieve' + 호 'protect, care for') and 실 (室, 'room').

굵다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 굵다 ('to be thick in girth or diameter, coarse').

history.meaning: thick (of cylinders, lines, raindrops, or voice)

굵다.notes: Contrasts with 두껍다, which measures flat thickness (books, walls, fabric).

굽다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 굽다 ('to roast, bake, grill over heat' [ㅂ-irregular: 구워]; or homophonous 'to be bent, curved' [regular: 굽어]).

history.meaning: to bake, roast, grill; to be curved

궁금해하다.etymology: Derived verb formed from 궁금하다 ('to be curious, wonder anxiously') + auxiliary -어하다, which converts an internal psychological adjective into a transitive/observable verb.

history.meaning: to wonder about, be curious about

귀.etymology: Native Korean body-part noun descending from Middle Korean 귀 ('ear').

규정.etymology: Sino-Korean 규정 (規定), compounding 규 (規, 'compass, standard, rule') and 정 (定, 'fix, establish, settle').

규칙.etymology: Sino-Korean 규칙 (規則), compounding 규 (規, 'compass, circle-standard') and 칙 (則, 'rule, law, norm').

균일하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 균일 (均一, 균 'equal, even' + 일 'one, uniform') + -하다.
균일하다.notes: Adverbial 균일하게 ('evenly, uniformly') is common in painting and baking instructions.

그.etymology: Native Korean medial demonstrative determiner and third-person pronoun descending from Middle Korean 그 ('that [near listener or already mentioned]; he/she').
그.notes: Forms the medial member of the Korean three-way demonstrative system 이 ('this') — 그 ('that near you / known') — 저 ('that over there').

그거.etymology: Colloquial contraction of the native Korean demonstrative pronoun 그것 (그 'that' + 거 < 것 'thing').

그것.etymology: Native Korean compound pronoun formed from medial demonstrative 그 ('that') + bound noun 것 ('thing, object'), attested since Middle Korean.

그냥.etymology: Contracted from 그 모양 (native 그 'that' + Sino-Korean 모양 模樣 'form, state, appearance'), literally 'in that state as it is'.

history.meaning: just, as it is, without any special reason

그다음.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining medial demonstrative 그 ('that') and 다음 ('next, following').

그대로.etymology: Native Korean compound adverb combining demonstrative 그 ('that') and particle/bound noun 대로 ('in accordance with, just as').

history.meaning: just as it is, intact, without change

그래도.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 그러하여도 / 그리하여도 (from 그러하다 'to be so' + concessive ending -어도).

그래서.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 그리하여서 / 그러하여서 (그러하다 'to be so, do so' + causal connective -어서).

그러니까.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 그러하니까 (그러하다 'to be so' + causal/explanatory ending -으니까).

history.meaning: therefore, so; I mean, that is to say

그러다.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative pro-verb contracted from 그러하다 / 그리하다 ('to do so, say so, be like that').

그러다가.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb formed from 그러다 ('to do so') + transfer/interruptive ending -다가.

그런.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative determiner contracted from 그러한, the adnominal form of 그러하다 ('to be like that, be such').

그런데.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 그러한데 (그러하다 'to be so' + circumstantial/contrastive ending -ㄴ데).

그럼.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb and interjection contracted from 그러면 ('if so, then') or from the substantive form 그러함 ('being so; of course').

history.meaning: then, in that case; of course

그렇게.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative adverb contracted from 그러하게 (그러하다 'to be like that' + adverbial ending -게).

history.meaning: like that, so, in that manner

그렇다.etymology: Native Korean ㅎ-irregular demonstrative adjective contracted from 그러하다 (Middle Korean 그러하다, from demonstrative 그 + -러- + 하다).

history.meaning: to be like that, be so
to be so, be like that

그릇.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 그릇 ('vessel, bowl, dish, container').

history.meaning: bowl, dish, vessel (also counter for servings)

그리고.etymology: Native Korean conjunction lexicalized from 그리하고 (그리하다 'to do so' + connective ending -고 'and').

그리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 그리다 ('to draw lines, paint a picture'; also homophonous with 그리다 'to yearn for, miss').

history.meaning: to draw, paint; to long for

그림.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun descending from Middle Korean 그림, derived from 그리다 ('to draw, paint') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

그림자.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 그리메 ('shadow, reflection'), formed from the root of 그리다 ('to outline, trace') + suffix -자.

그쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun and pronoun joining medial demonstrative 그 ('that') and 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: that side, that direction; you/your side

그해.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining medial demonstrative 그 ('that') with 해 ('year, sun').

근처.etymology: Sino-Korean 근처 (近處), compounding 근 (近, 'near, close') and 처 (處, 'place, locality').

글.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 글 ('writing, text, script, composition'), historically linked to the root of 그리다 ('to draw, inscribe').

글쎄요.etymology: Polite interjection formed from native discourse marker 글쎄 (contracted from 그러할세 / 그리할까, expressing hesitation) + polite particle -요.

history.meaning: well..., let me see, I am not sure (polite)

글씨.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 글시, from 글 ('writing') + 시 ('seed, form, style').

글씨체.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 글씨 ('handwriting, script') with Sino-Korean 체 (體, 'body, style, form').

글자.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound descending from Middle Korean 글짜, combining native 글 ('writing') with Sino-Korean 자 (字, 'letter, character').
글자.notes: Pronounced [글짜] with tensification reflecting the traditional compound link.

금.etymology: Represents both Sino-Korean 금 (金, 'gold, metal', from Middle Chinese *kim) and native Korean 금 (Middle Korean 금, 'drawn line, crease, crack, limit').

금고.etymology: Sino-Korean 금고 (金庫), compounding 금 (金, 'gold, money, valuables') and 고 (庫, 'storehouse, treasury, vault').

금방.etymology: Sino-Korean 금방 (今方), compounding 금 (今, 'now, this moment') and 방 (方, 'just now, right then').

history.meaning: just now; right away, very soon

금빛.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 금 (金, 'gold') with native 빛 ('light, color, gleam').

금색.etymology: Sino-Korean 금색 (金色), compounding 금 (金, 'gold') and 색 (色, 'color').

금속.etymology: Sino-Korean 금속 (金屬), compounding 금 (金, 'metal, gold') and 속 (屬, 'category, class').

금요일.etymology: Sino-Korean 금요일 (金曜日), from 금 (金, 'metal/gold, Venus') + 요 (曜, 'celestial luminary') + 일 (日, 'day').
금요일.notes: All seven days of the week in Korean end in 요일: 월요일 (Moon), 화요일 (Fire/Mars), 수요일 (Water/Mercury), 목요일 (Wood/Jupiter), 금요일 (Metal/Venus), 토요일 (Earth/Saturn), 일요일 (Sun).

금지.etymology: Sino-Korean 금지 (禁止), compounding 금 (禁, 'forbid, restrict') and 지 (止, 'stop, halt').

급하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 급 (急, 'urgent, pressing, hasty, steep') + native adjective-forming verb -하다.

history.meaning: to be urgent, hasty, in a hurry

급히.etymology: Derived adverb combining Sino-Korean 급 (急, 'urgent, hasty') with the native adverbial suffix -히.

기간.etymology: Sino-Korean 기간 (期間), compounding 기 (期, 'appointed time, term') and 간 (間, 'interval, span').

기관차.etymology: Sino-Korean 기관차 (機關車), from 기관 (機關, 'engine, mechanism') + 차 (車, 'wheeled vehicle, train car').

기꺼이.etymology: Native Korean adverb derived from the stem of 기껍다 (Middle Korean 깃겁다, 'to be glad, joyful') + adverbial suffix -이.

기다리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 기드리다 ('to wait for, await').

기대다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Early Modern Korean 기대다 ('to lean one's body or an object against a support').

history.meaning: to lean on, rest against, rely on

기대다.notes: Distinct from Sino-Korean 기대하다 (期待하다, 'to expect, look forward to').

기대하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 기대 (期待, 기 'expect, await a set time' + 대 'wait for') + -하다.
기대하다.notes: Conveys warm anticipation rather than mere neutral waiting.

기둥.etymology: Native Korean architectural noun descending from Middle Korean 기동 ('pillar, wooden column, post').

기록.etymology: Sino-Korean 기록 (記錄), compounding 기 (記, 'write down, note') and 록 (錄, 'inscribe, copy, register').

기름.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 기름 ('oil, fat, grease').

history.meaning: oil (cooking oil, lamp oil, or fuel)

기본.etymology: Sino-Korean 기본 (基本), compounding 기 (基, 'foundation, base') and 본 (本, 'root, origin, basis').

기쁘다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 깃브다, formed from the verb stem 깃- ('to rejoice') + adjective-forming suffix -브다.

기사님.etymology: Hybrid honorific title combining Sino-Korean 기사 (技士, 기 'skill, craft' + 사 'specialist', meaning 'technician, engineer, professional driver') with native honorific suffix -님.

기억.etymology: Sino-Korean 기억 (記憶), compounding 기 (記, 'remember, record') and 억 (憶, 'recall, keep in mind').

기억나다.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound verb combining Sino-Korean 기억 (記憶, 'memory') with native 나다 ('to arise, surface, come out').

history.meaning: to come to mind, be remembered

기억하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 기억 (記憶, 'memory, recollection') + native light verb -하다.

기울어지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 기울다 (Middle Korean 기울다, 'to tilt, incline') + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

history.meaning: to become tilted, lean over, slant

기울이다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 기우리다, formed from 기울다 ('to tilt, lean') + causative suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to cause to tilt or incline
to tilt, tip; to devote (attention or effort, e.g. 귀를 기울이다)

기지개.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 기지게 ('stretching one's body and limbs').

history.meaning: body stretch (idiomatic with 켜다: 기지개를 켜다)

기차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 기차 (汽車), literally 'steam vehicle', from 기 (汽, 'steam') + 차 (車, 'wheeled vehicle').
기차.notes: Remains the everyday Korean word for intercity trains even in the era of electric high-speed rail.

기차역.etymology: Sino-Korean 기차역 (汽車驛), combining 기차 (汽車, 기 'steam' + 차 'vehicle', 'train') and 역 (驛, 'post station, railway station').

기차표.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 기차표 (汽車票), joining 기차 (汽車, 'steam/rail train') with 표 (票, 'ticket, slip').
기차표.notes: Parallel to 입장표 ('admission ticket') and 차표 ('transit ticket').

긴장하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 긴장 (緊張, 긴 'tight, taut' + 장 'stretch a bowstring') + native light verb -하다.

history.meaning: to be nervous, tense up, stay on alert

길.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 길 (stem 길ㅎ, 'road, path, way, journey').

길다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem adjective descending from Middle Korean 길다 ('to be long in length or duration').

길이.etymology: Native Korean derived measure noun descending from Middle Korean 기리, formed from 길- (길다, 'to be long') + nominalizing suffix -이.

깊다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 깊다 ('to be deep, profound').

깎다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 깍다 ('to pare, whittle, peel, trim, lower a price').

깔끔하다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive adjective formed from expressive root 깔끔- ('neat, clean-cut, sharp') + -하다.

history.meaning: to be neat, tidy, clean and streamlined

깔다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 깔다 ('to spread out a mat, rug, or bedding underneath').

history.meaning: to spread out, lay down underneath
to spread, lay (a rug, sheet, floor), install

깜빡이다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from mimetic root 깜빡 ('momentary blink or flicker') + verbalizing suffix -이다.

깜빡하다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from mimetic root 깜빡 ('blinking shut; momentary lapse of awareness') + -하다.

history.meaning: to slip one's mind, momentarily forget; to blink/flicker

깜짝.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb descending from Middle Korean 감짝 ('with a sudden startle or flinch').

history.meaning: with a start, suddenly surprised (깜짝 놀라다)

깨끗이.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from the root 깨끗- of 깨끗하다 ('to be clean') + adverbial suffix -이.
깨끗이.notes: Takes -이 rather than -히 because the root ends in -ㅅ.

깨끗하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective attested from Early Modern Korean as 깨끝하다 / 깨끗하다 ('to be clean, unsoiled, tidy').

깨뜨리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb formed from 깨다 (Middle Korean 깨다, 'to break, shatter') + intensive transitive suffix -뜨리다.

깨우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb formed from 깨다 ('to wake from sleep, sober up') + causative suffix -우-.

깨지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive/passive verb formed from 깨다 ('to break, smash') + auxiliary suffix -지다.

history.meaning: to break, shatter, be chipped, fall through

꺼내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb contracted from 끌어내다 (Middle Korean 끄어내다, from 끌다/끄다 'to pull, draw' + 내다 'to put out').

history.meaning: to take out, pull out, bring up (a topic)

꺼지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb formed from 끄다 (Middle Korean 끄다, 'to extinguish, put out fire') + inchoative -어지다; also from 꺼지다 ('to sink in, cave in').

history.meaning: to be extinguished; to sink or collapse
to go out (of fire/light/power); to sink in, hollow out

껍질.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 겁질 ('outer skin, bark, rind, shell').

꼬마.etymology: Native Korean noun referring to a small child or miniature object, related to older Korean 고마 ('small or subordinate figure').

꼬집.etymology: Native Korean stem noun from 꼬집다 (Middle Korean 고집다, 'to pinch with thumb and fingertips'), used as a measure noun (한 꼬집 'a pinch').

history.meaning: pinch (unit of salt, spice, or powder)

꼭.etymology: Native Korean emphatic and mimetic adverb (light-vowel tensed form) meaning 'tightly, firmly; without fail, surely, exactly'.

history.meaning: tightly; surely, be sure to; exactly

꼭대기.etymology: Native Korean noun built from root 꼭- ('vertex, tip, crown', cf. 꼭지) + noun suffix -대기.

꽂다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 곶다 ('to stick in, insert upright, plant').

history.meaning: to stick in, slot in (books, flowers, plug)

꽃꿀.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound of 꽃 ('flower, blossom') and 꿀 ('honey, nectar').
꽃꿀.notes: Pronounced [꼳꿀] as final ㅊ neutralizes to [ㄷ] and tensifies the following ㄱ.

꽃집.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 꽃 (Middle Korean 곶, 'flower, blossom') and 집 ('house, shop').

꽉.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb meaning 'tightly, firmly, packed full to capacity'.

꽤.etymology: Native Korean degree adverb meaning 'quite, fairly, considerably more than expected'.

꾸다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 꾸다 ('to dream a dream'; also homophonous 'to borrow money or grain').

꾸러미.etymology: Native Korean derived noun from 꾸리다 ('to wrap up, pack, bundle') + nominal suffix -어미.

history.meaning: wrapped bundle or string of items

꿀.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 꿀 ('honey').

꿈.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun descending from Middle Korean 꿈, formed from 꾸다 ('to dream') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

꿈꾸다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb uniting the cognate object 꿈 ('dream') with its parent verb 꾸다 ('to dream').

꿈쩍.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb depicting a heavy or deliberate slight movement (most often in negative expressions like 꿈쩍도 안 하다 'not budge an inch').

history.meaning: with a slight budge or stir

끄덕이다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from mimetic root 끄덕 ('nodding up and down') + verbalizer -이다.

끈적거리다.etymology: Native Korean sensory verb formed from root 끈적 ('sticky, viscous, tacky') + iterative verbalizing suffix -거리다.

history.meaning: to be sticky, feel tacky or clammy

끊다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 끊다 / 그츠다 ('to sever, cut off, interrupt, stop').

history.meaning: to cut, sever, hang up, quit, buy (a ticket)

끔찍하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective attested in Early Modern Korean as 끔찍하다 ('startlingly intense, dreadful, terrible').

history.meaning: to be terrible, awful, ghastly; devoted (끔찍이)

끙.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic interjection and adverb imitating a suppressed groan of physical effort, strain, or ache.

끝.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 끝 / 귿 ('end, tip, extremity, conclusion').

끝나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 끝 ('end, finish') and 나다 ('to come out, come about').

끝부분.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 끝 ('end, tip') with Sino-Korean 부분 (部分, 'part, section').

끼다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 끼다 ('to become wedged between; to wear on hands/fingers/eyes; to gather [of mist/smoke/dust]').

history.meaning: to get stuck between; to put on (gloves/ring/glasses); to gather (fog/grime)

끼우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb derived from 끼다 ('to fit or wedge between') + causative suffix -우-.

history.meaning: to insert, slot in, fit into place

나.etymology: Native Korean first-person singular pronoun descending from Middle Korean 나 ('I, me').

history.meaning: I, me (plain/intimate; humble counterpart is 저)

나가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 나- (from 나다, 'to emerge, come out') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to go out, leave, attend, advance

나누다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 나노다 ('to divide, split, share').

history.meaning: to divide, split, share (food, conversation, feelings)

나눔.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 나누다 ('to divide, share') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

나다.etymology: Core native Korean intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 나다 ('to emerge, be born, sprout, happen, break out').

history.meaning: to come out, be born, arise
to come out, occur, sprout, break out

나머지.etymology: Native Korean derived noun formed from the stem 남- of 남다 ('to remain, be left over') + nominal suffix -어지.

나무.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 나모 (alternating stem 나모 / 남ㄱ, 'tree, wood, firewood').

나무살.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 나무 ('wood') and 살 ('spoke, lattice bar, strip').

history.meaning: wooden slat, lattice bar, wooden spoke

나뭇결.etymology: Native Korean compound of 나무 ('tree, wood') + genitive interfix 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 결 ('wave, grain, texture').
나뭇결.notes: Parallel to 물결 ('water wave') and 숨결 ('breathing rhythm').

나뭇잎.etymology: Native Korean compound noun from 나무 ('tree') + compound linker -ㅅ- (saisiot) + 잎 (Middle Korean 닢, 'leaf').
나뭇잎.notes: Pronounced [나문닙] via ㄴ-insertion of historical initial 닢.

나쁘다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 낟브다 ('to be insufficient, inferior, low in quality', from 낟- 'low/short' + -브다), which broadened in Modern Korean to mean 'bad'.

나사.etymology: Sino-Korean 나사 (螺絲), compounding 나 (螺, 'spiral shell, conch') and 사 (絲, 'thread, wire').

나사선.etymology: Sino-Korean 나사선 (螺絲線), combining 나사 (螺絲, 'screw') and 선 (線, 'line, ridge').

나오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 나- (from 나다, 'to emerge, come out') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to come out, appear, be served

나이.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 나 (stem 나ㅎ, 'age, years of life') + incorporated nominative/noun suffix -이.

난방.etymology: Sino-Korean 난방 (煖房), compounding 난 (煖, 'warm, heat') and 방 (房, 'room').

날.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 날 ('day, sky/weather; cutting blade edge; warp thread').

날씨.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 날 ('day, sky condition') + -씨 ('state, condition, manner').

날짜.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 날 ('day') with Sino-Korean 자 (字, 'character, numeral'), with tensification of ㅈ > ㅉ.

낡다.etymology: Native Korean adjective/verb descending from Middle Korean 낣다 ('to grow old and worn out, be dilapidated [of inanimate things]').

history.meaning: to be old, worn, weathered, outdated

낡다.notes: Used for objects, clothes, and buildings (contrasting with 늙다 for living beings).

남.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 남 ('other people, stranger, someone else'); also homophonous with Sino-Korean 남 (南 'south' or 男 'man, male').

남기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 남기다, formed from 남다 ('to remain, be left over') + causative suffix -기-.

history.meaning: to leave behind, cause to remain

남다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 남다 ('to remain, be left over, exceed').

남색.etymology: Sino-Korean 남색 (藍色), compounding 남 (藍, 'indigo plant and dye') and 색 (色, 'color').

남자.etymology: Sino-Korean 남자 (男子), compounding 남 (男, 'male, man') and 자 (子, 'person, son').

남쪽.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 남 (南, 'south') with native 쪽 ('side, direction').

납작하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective formed from mimetic root 납작 ('flat, low and pressed down') + adjective-forming -하다.

낮.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 낮 ('daytime, daylight hours, noon').

낮다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 낟다 / 낮다 ('to be low in height, level, or rank').

history.meaning: to be low (height, pitch, temperature, rank)

내.etymology: Native Korean first-person singular form descending from Middle Korean 내, representing either the contraction of 나의 ('my') or 나 + historical nominative -이 ('I' before 가).

내기.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 내다 ('to put out stakes, produce') + nominalizing suffix -기.

내내.etymology: Native Korean temporal adverb descending from Middle Korean 내내 ('all along, continuously from beginning to end').

history.meaning: throughout, the whole time, all along

내년.etymology: Sino-Korean 내년 (來年), compounding 내 (來, 'come, coming, next', via initial law from 래) and 년 (年, 'year').

내놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 내- (from 내다, 'to put out, bring forth') and 놓다 ('to put, place').

history.meaning: to put out and set down
to put out, set out, offer, put up for sale/rent

내다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 내다, originally the causative of 나다 ('to come out, arise') formed with -이-.

history.meaning: to cause to come out, produce, emit
to put out, make, pay, submit

내려가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 내려- (from 내리다, 'to descend') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to go down, step down, drop

내려놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 내려- (from 내리다, 'to lower') and 놓다 ('to put down, release').

history.meaning: to put down, set down, let go of

내려다보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 내려다- (내리다 'to go down' + directional transfer suffix -어다) + 보다 ('to look at').

내려다보이다.etymology: Native Korean passive/potential verb derived from 내려다보다 ('to look down at') + passive suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to be visible below, be overlooked (of a view)

내려앉다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 내려- (from 내리다, 'to descend, sink') and 앉다 ('to sit, settle').

history.meaning: to sink down, sag, collapse, alight

내려오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 내려- (from 내리다, 'to descend') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to come down, be handed down

내리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 나리다 ('to come down, fall from the sky, get off, lower').

history.meaning: to fall (rain/snow), get off, lower, brew (tea/coffee)

내일.etymology: Sino-Korean 내일 (來日), compounding 내 (來, 'coming, next') and 일 (日, 'day').

냄새.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 내 ('smoke, vapor, odor') via extended Early Modern Korean 내암새 > 냄새.

냅킨.etymology: Borrowed from English napkin, referring to a cloth or paper serviette used at the table.

냉장고.etymology: Sino-Korean 냉장고 (冷藏庫), from 냉장 (冷藏, 냉 'cold' + 장 'store, preserve') + 고 (庫, 'storehouse, cabinet').

너.etymology: Native Korean second-person singular plain pronoun descending from Middle Korean 너 ('thou, you').

너도밤나무.etymology: Native Korean compound tree name formed from 너 ('you') + -도 ('also, too') + 밤나무 ('chestnut tree'), literally 'you-too-chestnut-tree' from its chestnut-like nuts and foliage.

너머.etymology: Native Korean noun lexicalized from the infinitive 넘어 of 넘다 ('to cross over, pass beyond'), spelled phonemically to denote the space beyond a height or barrier.

history.meaning: beyond, the other side (of a mountain, wall, window, orshoulder)

너무.etymology: Native Korean degree adverb descending from Middle Korean 너모, derived from the verb stem 넘- of 넘다 ('to exceed, go over') + adverbial suffix -오.

너비.etymology: Native Korean measure noun descending from Middle Korean 너비, derived from the older stem 너브- of 넓다 ('to be wide') + nominalizing suffix -이.

넉.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral descending from Middle Korean 넉 ('four'), preserved before specific classifiers such as 달 ('month'), 장 ('sheet'), 잔 ('cup'), and 줄 ('row').

history.meaning: four (before select classifiers, e.g. 넉 달 'four months')

넉넉히.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from the root 넉넉- of 넉넉하다 ('to be ample, plenty, more than enough') + adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: generously, amply, with plenty to spare

넓다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 너브다 / 넓다 ('to be wide, broad, spacious').

넘기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 넘기다, formed from 넘다 ('to cross over, pass') + causative suffix -기-.

history.meaning: to pass over, cause to cross
to turn (a page), hand over, pass (a deadline or crisis)

넘다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 넘다 ('to cross over a height or boundary, exceed, overflow').

history.meaning: to cross over, exceed, pass beyond

넣다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 녀타 (녛다, 'to put inside, insert').

네.etymology: Polite Korean response interjection meaning 'yes, I see' (variant of 예); also homophonous with the adnominal numeral 네 ('four', from 넷) and pronoun 네 ('your' or 'you' < 너의 / 너+이).

history.meaning: band of fabric worn around the collar

넷.etymology: Native Korean cardinal numeral descending from Middle Korean 넿 / 넷 ('four').

년.etymology: Sino-Korean bound noun and counter 년 (年, 'year'), from Middle Chinese *nen.

노랗다.etymology: Native Korean ㅎ-irregular color adjective descending from Middle Korean 노라하다 ('to be bright yellow').

노래.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 노래 ('song'), historically derived from the root 놀- of 놀다 ('to play, sing, enjoy oneself').

노래하다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from 노래 ('song') + light verb -하다.

노릇노릇하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective built on 노릇- (related to 노랗다, 'yellowish, golden') + -하다, describing pleasantly browned or toasted surfaces.

history.meaning: to be nicely golden-brown (of baked or grilled food)

놀라다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 놀라다 ('to be startled, surprised, frightened').

높다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 높다 ('to be high, tall, elevated').

놓다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 노타 (놓다, 'to put down, set, release, let go').

history.meaning: to put, place, let go; auxiliary (-어 놓다) 'do and keep in state'

놓이다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb descending from Middle Korean 노히다, formed from 놓다 ('to place, release') + passive suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to be placed, lie on; to feel relieved (마음이 놓이다)

누가.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite subject pronoun formed from the older root 누 ('who', Middle Korean 누) + nominative particle 가.

누구.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite pronoun descending from Middle Korean 누고, formed from pronoun root 누 ('who') + interrogative ending -고.

누군가.etymology: Native Korean indefinite pronoun contracted from 누구인가 (누구 'who' + copula -이- + interrogative/indefinite ending -ㄴ가).

누르다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 누르다 ('to press down, push, suppress').

history.meaning: to press (a button or key), push down

눈.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from two Middle Korean words distinguished by pitch/vowel length: 눈 ('eye; bud, sprout') and 눈ː ('snow').

눈금자.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 눈금 (눈 'notch, mark' + 금 'line', 'scale division') and 자 (Middle Korean 자ㅎ, 'measuring stick, ruler').

눈빛.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 눈 ('eye') and 빛 ('light, gleam, expression').

history.meaning: gleam or look of the eyes
look in one's eyes, gaze, eye expression

느끼다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 늣기다 ('to sob, be emotionally moved'), which broadened in Modern Korean to mean 'to feel, sense, perceive'.

느리다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 느리다 ('to be slow, unhurried, slack').

느슨해지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 느슨하다 ('to be loose, slack', related to 늘다/느리다) + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

는.etymology: Native Korean topic and contrastive particle used after vowel-final words, descending from Middle Korean 난 / 는 (allomorph of 은).

늘.etymology: Native Korean temporal adverb meaning 'always, constantly', related to the verbal root 늘- ('to stretch, continue').

늦다.etymology: Native Korean adjective and verb descending from Middle Korean 늦다 ('to be late, tardy; to loosen').

님.etymology: Inherited from Middle Korean 님 (nim, 'lord, master, esteemed person'). Used in modern Korean as a polite honorific bound noun after names (지훈 님) and as an affix in titles such as 손님 ('guest') and 사장님 ('boss').
님.notes: Spelled with a space after personal names (지훈 님) and solid inside established titles (사장님, 선생님, 손님).

다.etymology: Native Korean degree and quantifier adverb descending from Middle Korean 다 ('all, completely, entirely').

다니다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 다니다 ('to walk about, go back and forth, frequent').

history.meaning: to go about, travel back and forth
to go back and forth, commute, attend

다들.etymology: Native Korean compound combining quantifier adverb 다 ('all') with plural marker -들.

다락방.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 다락 ('loft, raised storage space') with Sino-Korean 방 (房, 'room').
다락방.notes: Refers to a tucked-away attic or eaves room under the roof.

다루다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 다로다 ('to handle, work with, manage, train').

다르다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 다르다 ('to be different, distinct, other').

다리.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 다리 ('leg of a person, animal, or furniture; bridge spanning water').
다리.notes: Both 'leg' and 'bridge' reflect the shared concept of a connecting span or support.

다스.etymology: Borrowed via Japanese dāsu (ダース) from English dozen, denoting a set of twelve items (especially pencils or stationery).

다시.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 다시 ('again, once more, anew').

다음.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 다음, derived from the stem of 닿다/다으다 ('to adjoin, follow closely') + nominalizer -음.

다투다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 다토다 ('to contend, quarrel, compete, wrangle').

다툼.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 다투다 ('to quarrel, contend') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

다행.etymology: Sino-Korean 다행 (多幸), compounding 다 (多, 'much, great') and 행 (幸, 'good fortune, luck').

다행히.etymology: Derived adverb combining Sino-Korean 다행 (多幸, 'good fortune, relief') with native adverbial suffix -히.

닦다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 닥다 ('to wipe clean, polish, scrub, cultivate').

단단하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective formed from reduplicated root 단단- ('hard, solid, sturdy') + -하다.

history.meaning: to be hard, solid, sturdy, firm

단단해지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 단단하다 ('to be hard, solid') + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

history.meaning: to harden, become firm or solid

단단히.etymology: Native Korean derived adverb from 단단- ('hard, firm, solid') + adverbial suffix -히.

단위.etymology: Sino-Korean 단위 (單位), from 단 (單, 'single') + 위 (位, 'rank, position, standard place').
단위.notes: Follows metric or time nouns (밀리미터 단위, 분 단위) to mean 'by the unit of'.

단지.etymology: Represents both native Korean 단지 (Middle Korean 단지, 'bellied earthenware or glass jar/pot for honey, jam, or condiments') and Sino-Korean 단지 (但只 'merely, only'; 團地 'housing/industrial complex').

history.meaning: small jar, pot / only, merely / estate, complex

단호하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 단호 (斷乎, 단 'cut off, decide' + 호 classical descriptive suffix, 'resolute, decisive') + native adjective-forming -하다.

닫다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 닫다 ('to close, shut a door or lid').

닫히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb descending from Middle Korean 닫히다, formed from 닫다 ('to close, shut') + passive suffix -히-.
닫히다.notes: Pronounced [다치다] via regular aspiration and palatalization of ㄷ + 히.

달.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 달 ('moon; calendar month').

history.meaning: moon; month (used with native Korean numerals)

달다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem word descending from Middle Korean 달다, representing both the verb 'to hang, attach, install; to weigh' and the homophonous adjective 'to be sweet'.

history.meaning: to hang/attach; to weigh; to be sweet
to attach, hang up, put on; to be sweet

달리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 달리다, representing (1) 'to run, gallop, speed along' (from 닫다 'to run') and (2) the passive of 달다 ('to hang from, be attached to, depend on').

history.meaning: to run/gallop; to be hung or attached
to run, drive; to hang on, be attached to

달콤하다.etymology: Native Korean sensory adjective formed from the stem 달- of 달다 ('to be sweet') + expressive derivative suffix -콤하다.

닳다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 달타 (닳다, 'to wear down by friction, boil down, be worn out').

history.meaning: to wear down, become worn or frayed

담다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 담다 ('to put or fill into a vessel, dish, or bag').

history.meaning: to put in a dish/container; to capture or express (a story or feeling)

담당.etymology: Sino-Korean 담당 (擔當), compounding 담 (擔, 'carry on the shoulders, undertake') and 당 (當, 'take charge of, bear').

담벼락.etymology: Compound noun joining native 담 ('enclosure wall') and 벼락 (nativized colloquial expansion of Sino-Korean 벽 壁, 'wall face').

담요.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 담 (毯, 'woollen felt rug or blanket') with native 요 (Middle Korean 요, 'padded bedding mat').

담쟁이덩굴.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 담쟁이 (담 'wall' + -쟁이 'climber/dweller', 'Boston ivy') and 덩굴 ('vine, creeper').

당근.etymology: Sino-Korean 당근 (唐根), compounding 당 (唐, 'Tang China; imported/foreign') and 근 (根, 'root').

당기다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 당기다 ('to pull, draw toward oneself, tug').

history.meaning: to pull, draw near, move up (a time)

당연히.etymology: Derived adverb combining Sino-Korean 당연 (當然, 당 'ought, rightful' + 연 'so, thus') with the native adverbial suffix -히.

당장.etymology: Sino-Korean 당장 (當場), compounding 당 (當, 'this very, right at') and 장 (場, 'spot, place, occasion').

history.meaning: right now, immediately, on the spot

당황하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 당황 (唐皇, 'baffled and flustered') + native verb/adjective suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to be flustered, bewildered, taken aback

닿다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 다타 (닿다, 'to touch, reach, arrive at').

history.meaning: to touch, make contact with, reach

대.etymology: Represents both Sino-Korean bound noun/counter 대 (臺, 'platform, stand; counter for machines, vehicles, and pianos'; or 代, 'generation, era, price range') and native Korean 대 (Middle Korean 대, 'bamboo stalk, hollow stem, rod').

history.meaning: stand, machine counter / generation / bamboo stalk

대다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 대다 (causative of 닿다 'to touch, reach' formed with -이-).

history.meaning: to cause to touch or reach
to place/press against, supply, pull up (a vehicle)

대문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 대문 (大門), literally 'great gate', from 대 (大, 'big, main') + 문 (門, 'gate').
대문.notes: Refers to the main outer gate leading from the street into a house's courtyard.

대신.etymology: Sino-Korean 대신 (代身), compounding 대 (代, 'replace, substitute') and 신 (身, 'body, person').

history.meaning: substituting for a person or thing
instead of, in place of, substitute

대표.etymology: Sino-Korean 대표 (代表), compounding 대 (代, 'act in place of, represent') and 표 (表, 'surface, display, model').

대화.etymology: Sino-Korean 대화 (對話), compounding 대 (對, 'face each other') and 화 (話, 'speech, talk').

더.etymology: Native Korean comparative degree adverb descending from Middle Korean 더 ('more, further').

더하다.etymology: Native Korean verb and adjective formed from comparative adverb 더 ('more') + -하다 (replacing Middle Korean 더으다).

history.meaning: to add, increase; to grow more intense

덕분.etymology: Sino-Korean 덕분 (德分), compounding 덕 (德, 'virtue, kindness, favor') and 분 (分, 'allotted share, portion').

history.meaning: share of grace or favor received
thanks to, owing to (positive cause, especially in 덕분에)

덜거덕거리다.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic verb formed from root 덜거덕 ('rattling or clattering sound of loose hard objects') + iterative suffix -거리다.

덧문.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native prefix 덧- ('added over, outer layer') with Sino-Korean 문 (門, 'door').
덧문.notes: Pronounced [던문] by nasal assimilation of ㅅ [ㄷ] before ㅁ.

덧창.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native prefix 덧- ('added over, secondary') with Sino-Korean 창 (窓, 'window').

덩굴.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 덩굴 ('creeping or climbing plant stem, vine').

덮다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 덥다 / 덮다 ('to cover over, put a lid on, close').

history.meaning: to cover, close (a book or lid)

데.etymology: Native Korean bound noun descending from Middle Korean 대 ('place, spot, point, case').

데려가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 데려- (from 데리다, Middle Korean 다리다, 'to have someone accompany one') and 가다 ('to go').

데려다주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 데려다- (데리다 'to accompany' + transfer suffix -어다) + 주다 ('to give / do for someone').

history.meaning: to escort, walk or drive someone to a destination

데려오다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 데려- (from 데리다, 'to have someone accompany one') and 오다 ('to come').

데스크.etymology: Borrowed from English desk, used in Korean especially for a reception desk, front desk, or editorial desk.

history.meaning: table or counter for reception/office work

데시벨.etymology: Borrowed from English decibel (from Latin deci- 'one-tenth' + bel, named after Alexander Graham Bell).

데워지다.etymology: Native Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 데우다 ('to warm up, heat liquids or food', causative of 데다) + -어지다.

도.etymology: Represents the musical solfège loanword 도 (from Italian do, first note of the scale / C), Sino-Korean 도 (度 'degree of temperature/angle'; 道 'province, way'), and the native additive particle -도 ('also, too, even').

history.meaning: musical note C / degree / also, even

도대체.etymology: Sino-Korean 도대체 (都大體), from 도 (都, 'all, wholly') + 대체 (大體, 'main body, gist'), used adverbially to intensify a question.

history.meaning: in the main, all in all
on earth, in the world, what/why ever

도망가다.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound verb combining Sino-Korean 도망 (逃亡, 도 'flee' + 망 'run away, escape') with native 가다 ('to go').

도면.etymology: Sino-Korean 도면 (圖面), compounding 도 (圖, 'drawing, diagram, plan') and 면 (面, 'surface, sheet').

history.meaning: sheet with an architectural or engineering plan

도서관.etymology: Sino-Korean 도서관 (圖書館), from 도서 (圖書, 도 'chart, map' + 서 'book', 'books and documents') + 관 (館, 'public building, hall').

도와주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 도와- (infinitive of ㅂ-irregular 돕다, 'to help') and benefactive auxiliary 주다 ('to give, do for someone').

도입부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 도입부 (導入部), combining 도입 (導入, 'leading in, introduction') with suffix -부 (部, 'part, section').
도입부.notes: Refers to the opening passage of a musical work, essay, or novel.

도자기.etymology: Three-character Sino-Korean compound 도자기 (陶磁器), uniting 도기 (陶器, 'earthenware/stoneware') and 자기 (磁器, 'porcelain') under 기 (器, 'vessel, ware').
도자기.notes: Covers everything from rustic stoneware teacups to glazed porcelain electrical insulators.

도장.etymology: Sino-Korean 도장 (圖章), compounding 도 (圖, 'emblem, seal') and 장 (章, 'stamp, badge'); also homophonous with 도장 (塗裝, 'paint/varnish coating').

도착하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 도착 (到着, 도 'reach, arrive' + 착 'touch, land at') + native light verb -하다.

독서.etymology: Sino-Korean 독서 (讀書), literally 독 (讀, 'read aloud/study') + 서 (書, 'book, writing').
독서.notes: Classical East Asian compound used in modern Korean for reading books for pleasure or study.

독서등.etymology: Sino-Korean 독서등 (讀書燈), combining 독서 (讀書, 독 'read' + 서 'book') and 등 (燈, 'lamp, light').

돈.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 돈 ('money, coin; traditional unit of weight equal to 3.75 grams').

돋보기안경.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 돋보기 (돋- 'amplify/raise' + 보- 'see' + -기, 'magnifying glass') with Sino-Korean 안경 (眼鏡, 'eyeglasses').

돌.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 돌 (stem 돌ㅎ, 'stone, rock'); also homophonous with 돌 ('full year cycle, first birthday').

돌계단.etymology: Hybrid compound joining native Korean 돌 ('stone') with Sino-Korean 계단 (階段, 'stairs, steps').
돌계단.notes: Common in hillside lanes and courtyard entrances across older Seoul neighbourhoods.

돌길.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 돌 ('stone') and 길 ('road, path').

돌다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 돌다 ('to turn, revolve, spin, go around').

history.meaning: to turn, spin, go around, circulate

돌다리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 돌 ('stone') and 다리 ('bridge').
돌다리.notes: Famous in the proverb 돌다리도 두들겨 보고 건너라 ('Even a stone bridge, tap it before crossing' — look before you leap).

돌담.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 돌 ('stone') and 담 ('wall, enclosure fence').

돌려드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble compound verb joining 돌려- (from 돌리다, 'to turn/give back') and humble 드리다 ('to give to a respected person').

돌려보내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 돌려- (from 돌리다, 'to turn back') and 보내다 ('to send').

돌리다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 돌리다, formed from 돌다 ('to turn, spin') + causative suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to cause to turn or revolve
to turn, spin, run (an appliance), pass around

돌바닥.etymology: Native Korean compound of 돌 ('stone') and 바닥 ('floor, ground surface').
돌바닥.notes: Parallel to 돌계단 ('stone steps') and 마룻바닥 ('wooden floor').

돌벽.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound joining native 돌 ('stone') with Sino-Korean 벽 (壁, 'wall').
돌벽.notes: Pronounced [돌벽]; synonymous with pure-native 돌담 ('stone garden wall') when outdoors.

돌보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb contracted from 돌아보다 (돌다 'to turn toward' + 보다 'to look after').

history.meaning: to look back at, look after
to take care of, look after, tend

돌아가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 돌아- (from 돌다, 'to turn, circle') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to go back, return; to detour; to spin/operate

돌아서다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 돌아- (from 돌다, 'to turn around') and 서다 ('to stand').

history.meaning: to turn around, turn one's back, pivot

돌아오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 돌아- (from 돌다, 'to turn around') and 오다 ('to come').

돕다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 돕다 (stem 돕- > 도오- / 도와-, 'to help, assist').

동그라미.etymology: Native Korean noun derived from the descriptive stem 동그랗- ('to be round, circular') plus noun-forming suffix -미.
동그라미.notes: Contrasts bright-vowel 동그라미 ('neat small circle') with dark-vowel 둥근 ('broadly round').

동글동글하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective formed from light-vowel root 동글- (counterpart of 둥글다, 'round') + -하다.

history.meaning: to be nicely round, plump, or small and spherical

동네.etymology: Nativized Korean spelling of Sino-Korean 동내 (洞內, 동 'village, ward' + 내 'inside, within').

동료.etymology: Sino-Korean 동료 (同僚), compounding 동 (同, 'same, together') and 료 (僚, 'official, companion in office').

동생.etymology: Sino-Korean 동생 (同生), compounding 동 (同, 'same') and 생 (生, 'birth, born of the same parents'), which specialized in Korean from 'sibling' to 'younger sibling'.

history.meaning: sibling born of the same parents

동안.etymology: Korean temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 동안 ('interval of time or space, while').

history.meaning: during, for the duration of, while

동전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 동전 (銅錢), from 동 (銅, 'copper, bronze') and 전 (錢, 'coin, money').
동전.notes: Originally referred to cast copper coins; now denotes small metal change of any alloy.

되다.etymology: Core native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 다외다 (> 되다, 'to become, turn into, be completed').

history.meaning: to become, be done, work/function, reach

되찾다.etymology: Native Korean prefix 되- ('back again, reverse') + 찾다 ('to find, seek, retrieve').
되찾다.notes: Used both literally for recovering lost items and figuratively for regaining health or voice.

되풀이하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from prefix 되- ('again, back') + 풀이 (deverbal noun from 풀다, 'unfolding, performance') + -하다.

history.meaning: to repeat over and over, iterate

두.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral descending from Middle Korean 두 ('two' before nouns and classifiers, apocopated from 둘).

history.meaning: two (before counters/nouns, e.g. 두 개, 두 번)

두근거리다.etymology: Native Korean mimetic verb formed from root 두근 ('thumping of a beating heart') + iterative verbalizing suffix -거리다.

history.meaning: for the heart to thump repeatedly
to throb, palpitate, pound (of the heart)

두근두근하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic verb/adjective from 두근두근 ('pit-a-pat, thump-thump') + -하다.

history.meaning: for one's heart to pound with anticipation or nerves

두껍다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 둗겁다 ('to be thick in layer or flat depth').

history.meaning: to be thick (of walls, boards, books, fabric)

두다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 두다 ('to put, place, keep, leave in place').

history.meaning: to put, keep; resultative auxiliary (-어 두다) 'do in advance and keep'

두드리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 두드리다 ('to knock, tap, beat, hammer').

history.meaning: to knock on (a door), tap, drum

둘.etymology: Native Korean cardinal numeral descending from Middle Korean 둘 (stem 돓, 'two').

둘러보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 둘러- (from 두르다, 'to turn around, encircle') and 보다 ('to look, see').

둘째.etymology: Native Korean ordinal numeral formed from 둘 ('two') + ordinal suffix -째.

둥글다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem adjective descending from Middle Korean 둥글다 ('to be round, circular, spherical').

뒤.etymology: Native Korean spatial and temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 뒤 (stem 뒤ㅎ, 'back, rear, behind; after, later').

뒤돌아서.etymology: Native Korean participial/adverbial form built from 뒤 ('back') + 돌아서다 ('to turn around and stand') + connective -어.

history.meaning: turning around, having turned one's back

뒤집다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 드위집다 ('to turn upside down, flip over').

history.meaning: to turn over, flip, turn inside out

뒤쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 뒤 ('back, rear') and 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: the back side, toward the rear

뒷면.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 뒤 ('back') + compound linker -ㅅ- (saisiot) + Sino-Korean 면 (面, 'face, surface, page').
뒷면.notes: Pronounced [뒨면] via nasal assimilation across the compound boundary.

뒷문.etymology: Hybrid compound joining native 뒤 ('back, rear') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + Sino-Korean 문 (門, 'door, gate').
뒷문.notes: Pronounced [뒨문] by nasalization before ㅁ; contrasts with 앞문 ('front door') and 대문 ('main gate').

뒷부분.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 뒤 ('back, rear') + compound linker -ㅅ- (saisiot) + Sino-Korean 부분 (部分, 'part, section').

history.meaning: back part, rear section, latter part

드디어.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 드듸여, originally the infinitive form of 드듸다 ('to step on, tread upon'), grammaticalized into 'at last, finally'.

드라이버.etymology: Borrowed from English driver (in Korean hardware usage clipped from screwdriver via Japanese doraibā ドライバー).

history.meaning: tool for turning screws; vehicle driver

드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble verb descending from Middle Korean 드리다 (originally the causative of 들다 'to enter', meaning 'to cause an offering to enter a superior's presence').

history.meaning: to present or offer to a superior
to give, offer (humble counterpart of 주다)

드시다.etymology: Native Korean subject-honorific verb formed from 들다 ('to lift, take in hand, eat or drink') + honorific suffix -시-.

든든하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective formed from root 든든- ('firm, reassuring, well-filled') + -하다.

history.meaning: to feel reassured/secure; to feel satisfyingly full (of a meal)

듣다.etymology: Native Korean ㄷ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 듣다 (stem 듣- > 드러- before vowels, 'to hear, listen').

history.meaning: to hear, listen to (conjugates 들어 / 들으니)

들다.etymology: Core native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from two Middle Korean verbs distinguished by tone: 들다 (low tone, 'to enter, go inside, cost, contain') and 들다 (high tone, 'to lift, hold in one's hand').

history.meaning: to enter, go in / to lift, hold
to enter, cost, set in; to hold, lift, carry

들려주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 들려- (from 들리다, causative of 듣다, 'to let someone hear') and benefactive 주다 ('to give').

history.meaning: to tell (a story), play (music or a sound) for someone

들리다.etymology: Native Korean passive and causative verb descending from Middle Korean 들리다, formed from 듣다 ('to hear') + suffix -리- (or from 들다 'to lift' + -리-).

history.meaning: to be heard, let hear; to be lifted
to be heard, sound audible; to be lifted

들보.etymology: Native Korean architectural compound combining 들- (from 들다, 'to hold up, suspend across') and 보 (Middle Korean 보, 'crossbeam').

history.meaning: main ceiling beam, girder, tie beam

들어가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 들어- (from 들다, 'to enter') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to go in, enter, fit inside, be required

들어오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 들어- (from 들다, 'to enter') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to come in, enter (toward the speaker)

들여놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 들여- (from 들이다, causative of 들다, 'to bring inside') and 놓다 ('to put, place').

history.meaning: to bring inside and place (furniture, plants, or goods)

들이다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 드리다, formed from 들다 ('to enter, go in') + causative suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to cause to enter, let in

듯하다.etymology: Native Korean auxiliary adjective formed from the bound noun 듯 (Middle Korean 듯, 'seeming appearance, likelihood') + -하다.

history.meaning: to seem like, appear to be

등기.etymology: Sino-Korean 등기 (登記), compounding 등 (登, 'ascend, enter in an official register') and 기 (記, 'record, write down').

history.meaning: official entry in a public register

등불.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound descending from Middle Korean 등ㅅ불, combining Sino-Korean 등 (燈, 'lamp, lantern') with native 불 ('fire, light').

디딤판.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 디딤 (deverbal noun from 디디다, 'to step on, tread') with Sino-Korean 판 (板, 'board, plank, plate').

딛다.etymology: Native Korean verb contracted from 디디다 (Middle Korean 드듸다, 'to step on, tread on, set foot upon').

history.meaning: to step on, set foot on

따뜻하다.etymology: Native Korean temperature adjective descending from Early Modern Korean 따듯하다 (tensed counterpart of Middle Korean 다슷하다, 'warm, genial').

history.meaning: to be warm (of weather, objects, or heart)

따뜻해지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 따뜻하다 ('to be warm') + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

따라오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 따라- (from 따르다, 'to follow') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to follow (toward the speaker), come along with

따르다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from two Middle Korean verbs that merged in form: 따르다 ('to follow, accompany, abide by') and 떠르다 ('to pour liquid into a cup or vessel').

history.meaning: to follow, accompany / to pour liquid
to follow, comply with; to pour (tea, water, wine)

딱.etymology: Native Korean mimetic and degree adverb meaning 'with a sharp snap/crack; right on the mark, exactly, firmly'.

history.meaning: precisely, just, firmly; with a snap/thwack

딱딱하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective formed from root 딱딱- ('hard, solid, stiff, unyielding') + -하다.

딱딱해지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 딱딱하다 ('to be hard, stiff') + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

history.meaning: to harden, grow stiff or stale

딸기잼.etymology: Hybrid compound combining native Korean 딸기 (Middle Korean 떨기, 'berry, strawberry') with English loanword 잼 (jam).

딸깍.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic adverb imitating the crisp metallic click of a latch, lock, or switch.

history.meaning: clicking or rattling sound of a small hard object
click, clack (of a latch, key, or switch)

때.etymology: Native Korean temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 때 ('time, moment, season, mealtime').

때문.etymology: Native Korean bound noun attested from Early Modern Korean as 때문 ('reason, cause, ground', almost always used with 에 or 이다).

history.meaning: because of, on account of (bound noun)

떠나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 떠나다, formed from 뜨다 ('to rise, lift off from a spot') + 나다 ('to go out, emerge').

history.meaning: to rise and depart from a place

떠들썩하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective derived from the stem of 떠들다 ('to make noise, chatter loudly') + expressive suffix -썩하다.

history.meaning: to be noisy, bustling, abuzz, uproarious

떨리다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive/passive verb descending from Middle Korean 떨리다, formed from 떨다 ('to shake, shiver') + suffix -리-.

떨어뜨리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb formed from 떨어- (stem of 떨어지다, 'to fall') + intensive causative suffix -뜨리다.

떨어지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 떨어디다, from 떨다 ('to shake off, knock down') + auxiliary -어디다 (> -어지다).

history.meaning: to fall, drop; to run out of; to be some distance away

떼다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 떼다 ('to detach, pull off, separate').

history.meaning: to take off, peel off, remove (a label, seal, or gaze)

또.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 또 ('again, also, furthermore').

또렷하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective formed from expressive root 또렷- (light-vowel counterpart of 뚜렷-, 'clear, distinct, sharp') + -하다.

history.meaning: to be clear, distinct, vivid, sharp

똑같다.etymology: Native Korean compound adjective combining emphatic adverb 똑 ('precisely, just') with 같다 ('to be the same').

똑똑하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective formed from root 똑똑- ('clear, distinct, bright, sharp-witted') + -하다.

history.meaning: to be smart, clever, bright; clear/distinct

똑바로.etymology: Native Korean compound adverb combining emphatic 똑 ('precisely, right') with 바로 ('straight, directly, upright').

뚜껑.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 둿거우 / 뚜껑 (historically related to 덮다, 'to cover').

뛰다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 뛰다 ('to jump, leap, run; for the pulse/heart to beat').

history.meaning: to run, jump, leap; to beat (of the heart)

뛰어가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 뛰어- (from 뛰다, 'to run') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to run (toward a destination), go running

뜨거워지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 뜨겁다 ('to be hot') + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

뜨겁다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 뜨겁다 ('to be hot to the touch, ardent').

뜻.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 뜻 ('mind, intention, will, meaning').

라고.etymology: Native Korean quotative particle used after vowel-final nouns (allomorph of 이라고) or in direct/indirect quotation (-라고 하다), combining declarative -라 and quotative -고.

라디에이터.etymology: Borrowed from English radiator (from Latin radiāre, 'to emit rays/heat').

history.meaning: heating appliance or cooling heat exchanger

라벨.etymology: Borrowed from English label (influenced by continental European/Japanese pronunciation raberu), referring to an identifying tag or sticker.

history.meaning: identifying slip or sticker attached to an object

랜턴.etymology: Borrowed from English lantern (ultimately via Old French from Latin lanterna).

러그.etymology: Borrowed from English rug, denoting a thick woven floor mat or small carpet.

레.etymology: Borrowed from Italian musical solfège re, the second degree of the diatonic scale (or pitch D).

레몬.notes: Word-initial English l is written with ㄹ in Korean loanwords.
