레이스.etymology: Borrowed from English lace ('delicate openwork fabric', via Old French las from Latin laqueus 'noose, snare'); also homophonous with English race.

렌즈.etymology: Borrowed from English lens (from Latin lēns, 'lentil', because a double-convex glass lens resembles the shape of a lentil seed).

history.meaning: lens (optical lens, camera lens, contact lens)

렌치.etymology: Borrowed from English wrench, a hand tool used to grip and turn nuts or bolts.

history.meaning: tool for turning nuts and bolts

렌틸콩.etymology: Hybrid compound combining English loanword 렌틸 (lentil, from Old French lentille < Latin lēns) with native Korean 콩 ('bean, legume').
렌틸콩.notes: Shares its ultimate Latin root lēns ('lentil') with 렌즈 (lens), named for its biconvex lentil shape.

로비.etymology: Borrowed from English lobby, referring to the entrance hall or foyer of a hotel, theater, or large building.

롤.etymology: Borrowed from English roll, referring to a cylindrical roll of paper, fabric, or bread.

history.meaning: something rolled into a cylinder; bread roll

를.etymology: Native Korean accusative (direct object) case particle used after vowel-final nouns, descending from Middle Korean 랄 / 를 (allomorph of 을).

리듬.etymology: Borrowed from English rhythm (ultimately from Ancient Greek rhythmós, 'measured motion, symmetry').

리본.etymology: Borrowed from English ribbon, referring to a narrow strip of fabric tied in a bow or used as trim.

링.etymology: Borrowed from English ring, denoting a circular metal band, hoop, or key ring.

마다하다.etymology: Native Korean verb lexicalized from 말다 ('to desist, decline') + declarative/quotative -다 + 하다 (literally 'to say no to, decline to do').

history.meaning: to refuse, turn down, shrink from (often in 마다하지 않다 'not hesitate/refuse')

마디.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 마대 ('joint or node of bamboo/bone; knot; musical measure; phrase of speech').

history.meaning: joint, node; musical bar/measure; word/phrase (한 마디)

마룻바닥.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 마루 (Middle Korean 마루, 'raised wooden floor') + compound linker -ㅅ- (saisiot) + 바닥 ('floor, bottom surface').

마르다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 마르다 ('to become dry, dry up, grow thin').

history.meaning: to dry, run dry, become thin

마법.etymology: Sino-Korean 마법 (魔法), compounding 마 (魔, 'demon, supernatural spirit') and 법 (法, 'art, method, law').

마시다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 마시다 ('to drink liquid, breathe in').

마음.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 마음 ('heart, mind, inner spirit, intention').

마주.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 마조, derived from the stem 맞- of 맞다 ('to face, meet') + adverbial suffix -오/-우.

history.meaning: face to face, opposite each other

마지막.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'the last, final moment or item', formed from the stem of 마치다/맞다 ('to finish, conclude') + nominal suffix -막.

마침.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 마참 / 마침, related to 맞다 ('to fit the moment, hit the mark') and 마치다 ('to finish').

history.meaning: just then, opportunely, as it happened

마트.etymology: Borrowed from English mart (popularized in South Korea via discount-store chains and clipped from supermarket).

막다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 막다 ('to block, stop up, obstruct, keep out').

history.meaning: to block, stop, prevent, shield from

막히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb descending from Middle Korean 막히다, formed from 막다 ('to block') + passive suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be blocked, clogged, congested, deadlocked

만.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 만 (萬, 'ten thousand, 10,000'), from Middle Chinese *mjonH; also homophonous with the native restrictive particle/bound noun 만 ('only, just; elapsed time since').

history.meaning: ten thousand (10,000); only/just; after an interval of

만나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 맛나다, formed from 맞- ('to face, meet') + 나다 ('to come forth, occur'), with nasal assimilation of ㅅ + ㄴ > ㄴ + ㄴ.

만남.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 만나다 ('to meet') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

만들다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 맹글다 / 만들다 ('to make, craft, build, form').

만실.etymology: Sino-Korean 만실 (滿室), compounding 만 (滿, 'full') and 실 (室, 'room, guestroom').

만약.etymology: Sino-Korean 만약 (萬若), compounding 만 (萬, 'ten thousand [possibilities]') and 약 (若, 'if, suppose').

history.meaning: if by one chance in ten thousand
if, in case, by any chance

만점.etymology: Sino-Korean 만점 (滿點), compounding 만 (滿, 'full, complete') and 점 (點, 'point, score, mark').

history.meaning: full marks, perfect score, ten out of ten

말씀.etymology: Native Korean noun derived from 말 ('speech, words') with the historical nominalizing suffix -ᄊᆞᆷ / -씀, attested in 15th-century Hunminjeongeum texts as 말ᄊᆞᆷ.
말씀.notes: In modern Korean, 말씀 both elevates an elder's or guest's words (선생님 말씀) and humbles one's own (제가 말씀드릴게요).

메아리.etymology: Native Korean, from Middle Korean 뫼ᅀᅡ리 (mwǒyzàlí), which Wiktionary analyses as 'one who lives in the mountains' (뫼 'mountain' + 살- 'live' + agentive -이).
메아리.notes: The echo was pictured as a voice answering from the mountains.

목공풀.etymology: Hybrid compound of Sino-Korean 목공 (木工, 'woodworking, carpentry') and native 풀 ('glue, paste').
목공풀.notes: Pronounced [목꽁풀] with compound tensification of 목 + 공.

목소리.etymology: Native Korean compound of 목 ('throat, neck') and 소리 ('sound').
목소리.notes: Distinguishes a human speaking or singing voice from general 소리 ('sound, noise').

목요일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 목요일 (木曜日), built from 목 (木, 'tree, wood / Jupiter'), 요 (曜, 'luminary'), and 일 (日, 'day').
목요일.notes: Pronounced [모교일] via smooth liaison of final ㄱ onto initial ㅇ.

미완성.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 미완성 (未完成), attaching negative prefix 미- (未, 'not yet') to 완성 (完成, 'completion').

발가락.etymology: Native Korean compound of 발 ('foot') and 가락 ('slender stick, spindle, digit').
발가락.notes: Built on the exact same pattern as 손가락 ('finger', 손 'hand' + 가락) and 젓가락 ('chopsticks').

발걸음.etymology: Native Korean compound of 발 ('foot') and 걸음 ('step, gait', nominalized with -음 from 걷다 'to walk').
발걸음.notes: Describes both audible footsteps and the tempo of someone's walk.

발뒤꿈치.etymology: Native Korean compound of 발 ('foot') + 뒤 ('back, rear') + 꿈치 ('protruding joint bend', cf. 팔꿈치 'elbow').
발뒤꿈치.notes: Clearly distinguishes the heel of the foot from the heel of a shoe (굽).

발목.etymology: Native Korean anatomical compound of 발 ('foot') and 목 ('neck, narrow constriction').

발판.etymology: Hybrid compound combining native 발 ('foot') with Sino-Korean 판 (板, 'wooden board, plank').
발판.notes: Refers both to a low kitchen step stool and figuratively to a stepping-stone.

방석.etymology: Sino-Korean 방석 (方席), from 방 (方, 'square') + 석 (席, 'woven mat, seat').
방석.notes: Originally a square sedge or silk floor mat, now used for any square chair or floor cushion.

백설탕.etymology: Sino-Korean 백설탕 (白雪糖), prefixing 백- (白, 'white') to 설탕 (雪糖, 'snow-sugar').
백설탕.notes: Contrasts with 흑설탕 ('dark brown sugar') and 황설탕 ('golden raw sugar').

버터.etymology: Borrowed from English butter, following standard Korean loanword orthography based on non-rhotic vowel endings (-er -> -어).
버터.notes: Combines with Sino-Korean prefixes such as 무염 버터 ('unsalted butter').

보금자리.etymology: Native Korean compound historically referring to a bird's warm nest, formed with 자리 ('place, spot').
보금자리.notes: Used figuratively in modern Korean for a cosy home or welcoming workplace where one settles in.

보일러.notes: In South Korea, 보일러 specifically evokes the household hot-water and underfloor heating (온돌) boiler found in every home and guesthouse.

부담.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 부담 (負擔), from 부 (負, 'carry on the back') and 담 (擔, 'shoulder a load').
부담.notes: Both characters depict bearing physical weight, extended to emotional or financial pressure.

부엌문.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound joining native 부엌 ('kitchen') with Sino-Korean 문 (門, 'door').
부엌문.notes: Pronounced [부엉문]: final ㅋ neutralizes to [ㄱ] and assimilates to velar nasal [ㅇ] before ㅁ.

분필.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 분필 (粉筆), from 분 (粉, 'powder') and 필 (筆, 'writing brush, pen').
분필.notes: Shares 필 (筆, 'writing implement') with 연필 (鉛筆, 'pencil').

불투명.etymology: Sino-Korean negator 불- (不, 'not') prefixed to 투명 (透明, 'transparent': 투 透 'pass through' + 명 明 'bright, clear').
불투명.notes: Describes frosted conservatory or lamp glass that diffuses light without allowing a direct view through.

비교하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 비교 (比較, 비 'compare side by side' + 교 'measure against') + -하다.

비눗물.etymology: Korean compound of 비누 ('soap', an early loanword via Portuguese sabão) + compound linker 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + native 물 ('water').
비눗물.notes: Pronounced [비눈물] as 사이시옷 triggers nasal insertion before ㅁ.

비상용.etymology: Sino-Korean 비상 (非常, literally 'not ordinary' -> 'emergency') plus suffix -용 (用, 'for the use of').
비상용.notes: Productive -용 (用) suffix also forms 가정용 ('household use') and 상업용 ('commercial use').

빗방울.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound of 비 ('rain') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 방울 ('drop, bead').
빗방울.notes: Shares 비 + 사이시옷 with 빗물 ('rainwater') and 빗소리 ('sound of rain').

빗소리.etymology: Native Korean compound from 비 ('rain') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 소리 ('sound').
빗소리.notes: The linking ㅅ tenses the following consonant in speech: [빋쏘리].

빵.etymology: Borrowed via Japanese パン (pan) from 16th-century Portuguese pão ('bread'), ultimately from Latin pānis.
빵.notes: One of the earliest European-root loanwords in Korean, spelled with tense ㅃ to reflect the unaspirated Romance p.

사장.etymology: Sino-Korean 사장 (社長), from 사 (社, 'company, enterprise') + 장 (長, 'head, chief').
사장.notes: With honorific -님 (사장님), it is the universal polite title for shop, café, and guesthouse owners.

사장님.etymology: Combines Sino-Korean 사장 (社長, 'company president, shop proprietor') with the native honorific suffix -님.
사장님.notes: In everyday Seoul life, 사장님 politely addresses both a workplace boss and any café, restaurant, or shop owner.

사장조.etymology: Korean musical key name joining pitch letter 사 ('G', 7th of 가나다라마바사 = A–G) with Sino-Korean 장조 (長調, 'major key').
사장조.notes: Contrasts with 사단조 (g minor, 短調).

사촌.etymology: Sino-Korean kinship term 사촌 (四寸), literally 'four joints/degrees of kinship'.
사촌.notes: Traditional Korean kinship counts degrees (촌): parents-to-child is 1, siblings are 2, aunts/uncles are 3, and first cousins are 4 (사촌).

산꿀.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean compound joining Sino-Korean 산 (山, 'mountain') with native 꿀 ('honey').
산꿀.notes: Refers to dark, aromatic wildflower and chestnut honey harvested from mountain apiaries.

새하얗다.etymology: Native Korean intensifying colour prefix 새- ('vividly, dazzlingly') + 하얗다 ('white').

생나무.etymology: Hybrid compound combining Sino-Korean prefix 생- (生, 'raw, unseasoned, bare') with native 나무 ('tree, wood').
생나무.notes: Refers either to freshly cut green timber or to bare wood with no lacquer or paint.

서울.etymology: Native Korean proper name meaning 'capital city', widely connected by historical linguists through Middle Korean 셔ᄫᅳᆯ (syeweul) to Old Korean 서라벌 (Seorabeol), the capital of Silla.
서울.notes: Uniquely among East Asian capitals, 서울 is a native vernacular word rather than a Sino-Korean character compound.

선명하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 선명 (鮮明, 선 'fresh, vivid' + 명 'bright, clear') + -하다.
선명하다.notes: Describes vivid paint colours, sharp photographs, or crisp lettering.

선생님.etymology: Hybrid respectful title combining Sino-Korean 선생 (先生, literally 'born earlier', i.e. teacher/elder) with the native Korean honorific suffix -님.
선생님.notes: Addresses teachers, doctors, and respected older guests warmly and politely.

선풍기.etymology: Sino-Korean 선풍기 (扇風機), combining 선 (扇, 'fan') + 풍 (風, 'wind') + 기 (機, 'machine').
선풍기.notes: Pronounced [선풍기]; contrasts with 부채 (handheld paper/bamboo fan).

설탕.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 설탕 (雪糖), literally 'snow sugar', from 설 (雪, 'snow') and 당/탕 (糖, 'sugar').
설탕.notes: Named for the fine white crystals of refined sugar resembling fresh snow.

손가락.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound of 손 ('hand') and 가락 ('slender stick, spindle, or digit').
손가락.notes: The same native element 가락 appears in 발가락 ('toe'), 젓가락 ('chopsticks'), and 숟가락 ('spoon').

손글씨.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 손 ('hand') and 글씨 ('written letters, handwriting', derived from 글 'writing').
손글씨.notes: Contrasts personal pen-and-pencil script with printed type.

손잡이.etymology: Native Korean synthetic compound from 손 ('hand') + 잡- ('grip, hold') + nominalizing suffix -이: literally 'hand-holder'.
손잡이.notes: Covers door handles, suitcase handles, and teacup handles alike.

수성.etymology: Sino-Korean 수성 (水性), compounding 수 (水, 'water') + 성 (性, 'nature, property').
수성.notes: Used before 페인트 ('water-based paint') and 펜 ('water-based ink pen').

수수께끼.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in early modern Korean texts in forms such as 수수격기, meaning a verbal riddle or puzzle.
수수께끼.notes: Used both for word riddles and figuratively for a mysterious note or situation.

수첩.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수첩 (手帖), combining 수 (手, 'hand') and 첩 (帖, 'folded booklet, register').
수첩.notes: Literally a 'hand-booklet' small enough to slip into a coat or apron pocket.

숙박부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숙박부 (宿泊簿), from 숙박 (宿泊, 'lodging overnight') and 부 (簿, 'ledger, register book').
숙박부.notes: Shares 부 (簿, 'record book') with 장부 (帳簿, 'account ledger').

순간.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 순간 (瞬間), from 순 (瞬, 'blink of an eye') and 간 (間, 'interval of time').
순간.notes: Literally 'the space of a single blink'.

승진하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound joining 승진 (昇進, from 昇 'ascend, rise' + 進 'advance') with native light verb -하다.
승진하다.notes: Used seriously for workplace promotions and playfully for 'getting promoted' to taste tester.

시간.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시간 (時間), from 시 (時, 'time, hour') and 간 (間, 'interval, space between').
시간.notes: Means both 'time' in general and a duration of hours when preceded by a native Korean number (두 시간, 'two hours').

시간표.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 시간표 (時間表): 시간 ('time') + 표 (表, 'chart, table').
시간표.notes: Used for train timetables, bus schedules, and school class schedules.

시계.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시계 (時計), literally 'time-measurer', from 시 (時, 'time') + 계 (計, 'measure, gauge').
시계.notes: Covers both wall clocks and wristwatches.

시식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시식 (試食), from 시 (試, 'test, try') and 식 (食, 'eat, food').
시식.notes: Parallel to 시음 (試飮, 'drink tasting') and 시연 (試演, 'trial performance').

시청.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시청 (市廳), from 시 (市, 'city, municipality') and 청 (廳, 'government hall, administrative office').
시청.notes: In Seoul, 시청 refers both to City Hall itself and the major subway junction beside Seoul Plaza.

식빵.etymology: Hybrid compound prefixing Sino-Korean 식- (食, 'meal, staple food') to 빵 ('bread', borrowed via Japanese pan from Portuguese pão).
식빵.notes: Refers specifically to an unsweetened rectangular loaf sliced for toast or sandwiches.

식초.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식초 (食醋), from 식 (食, 'edible, food') and 초 (醋, 'vinegar, sour liquor').
식초.notes: Adding 식 (食) clarifies culinary vinegar in spoken Korean.

신문지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 신문지 (新聞紙), adding 지 (紙, 'paper') to 신문 (新聞, literally 'newly heard things' -> 'newspaper').
신문지.notes: Distinguishes physical sheets of newsprint (used for wrapping pottery or vegetables) from 신문 as a publication.

실례.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 실례 (失禮), literally 'losing courtesy' or 'a breach of etiquette'.
실례.notes: Pronounced [실례] by liquidization of ㄴ+ㄹ -> ㄹ+ㄹ; used in 실례합니다 and 실례지만 ('excuse me').

안경.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안경 (眼鏡), literally 'eye-mirror/lens', from 안 (眼, 'eye') + 경 (鏡, 'mirror, lens').
안경.notes: Takes the verb 쓰다 ('안경을 쓰다') when putting glasses on.

안녕하세요.etymology: Built from Sino-Korean 안녕 (安寧, 'peace and well-being'), the adjective-forming verb 하다, and the polite honorific ending -세요 (contracted from -시어요). Literally asks or wishes 'Are you at peace?'.
안녕하세요.notes: Used across South Korea at any hour of the day as the standard polite greeting.

안마당.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 안 ('inside, inner') with 마당 ('courtyard, yard').
안마당.notes: Traditional Korean courtyard houses arrange rooms around a sheltered 안마당 open to the sky.

약속.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 약속 (約束), combining 약 (約, 'bind, agree') and 속 (束, 'tie, bundle').
약속.notes: Covers both a personal promise ('약속해요!') and a scheduled appointment or plan with someone.

양모.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 양모 (羊毛), from 양 (羊, 'sheep') and 모 (毛, 'hair, wool, fur').
양모.notes: Dense compressed 양모 forms the felt hammers inside acoustic pianos.

얼음.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 얼다 ('to freeze') + nominalizing suffix -음.
얼음.notes: Retains morphophonemic spelling 얼음 (pronounced [어름]) showing its derivation from 얼-.

열쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound built from the prospective stem 열- of 열다 ('to open') and 쇠 ('iron, metal'): literally 'opening-metal'.
열쇠.notes: Pairs naturally with 잠그다 ('to lock') and 열다 ('to open').

영업하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 영업 (營業, 영 'manage, run' + 업 'business, trade') + -하다.
영업하다.notes: Standard term on Korean shopfront signs (영업중 'Open', 매일 영업합니다 'Open Daily').

예산.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 예산 (豫算), combining 예 (豫, 'beforehand, in advance') and 산 (算, 'count, calculate').
예산.notes: Shares the calculation root 산 (算) with 계산 ('payment / calculation').

예약.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 예약 (豫約), from 예 (豫, 'beforehand, in advance') and 약 (約, 'agreement, booking').
예약.notes: Standard noun for hotel, restaurant, and train reservations; pairs with 하다 ('예약하다').

온기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 온기 (溫氣), joining 온 (溫, 'warm, gentle') and 기 (氣, 'air, breath, energy').
온기.notes: Shares 온 (溫) with 온실 ('conservatory / greenhouse', 溫室).

온실.notes: Used for plant greenhouses and for glass sunrooms; the same 室 'room' appears in 사무실 'office' and 지하실 'basement'.

왼손.etymology: Native Korean compound of adnominal prefix 왼- ('left') and 손 ('hand').
왼손.notes: Pairs with 오른손 ('right hand') and 왼쪽 ('left side').

유리.etymology: Sino-Korean 琉璃, borrowed from Chinese 琉璃 'glass, glaze'.
유리.notes: Found in 유리창 'glass window' and 유리컵 'drinking glass'.

유리병.etymology: Compound of 유리 (琉璃, an ancient Buddhist Sanskrit loanword via Classical Chinese meaning 'lapis / glass') and 병 (瓶, 'bottle, jar').
유리병.notes: Used in everyday Korean for both narrow-necked glass bottles and wide-mouthed honey or jam jars.

음성.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음성 (音聲), uniting 음 (音, 'sound') and 성 (聲, 'voice').
음성.notes: Used in technical or formal contexts like 음성 메시지 ('voice message'), whereas native 목소리 is everyday spoken 'voice'.

음악.notes: The everyday word for music of any kind.

음표.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음표 (音標), combining 음 (音, 'sound, musical tone') and 표 (標, 'mark, symbol').
음표.notes: Shares 음 (音) with 음악 ('music') and 표 (標) with 화살표 ('arrow mark').

이슬비.etymology: Native Korean compound of 이슬 ('morning dew') and 비 ('rain').
이슬비.notes: Evokes a mist-like drizzle gentler than 소나기 ('passing shower') or 폭우 ('downpour').

일기예보.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound 일기예보 (日氣豫報), joining 일기 (日氣, 'daily weather') with 예보 (豫報, 'advance report, forecast').
일기예보.notes: Standard broadcast and everyday term for a weather forecast.

작곡가.etymology: Three-part Sino-Korean compound 작곡가 (作曲家): 작 (作, 'make, create') + 곡 (曲, 'tune, piece of music') + specialist suffix -가 (家).
작곡가.notes: Parallels 건축가 (建築家, 'architect') in using -가 (家) for an accomplished practitioner.

장부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 장부 (帳簿), combining 장 (帳, 'account register') and 부 (簿, 'record book, ledger').
장부.notes: Used for traditional paper account books and guesthouse check-in ledgers.

장인.etymology: Sino-Korean 장인 (匠人), from 장 (匠, 'artisan, master woodworker') + 인 (人, 'person').
장인.notes: Honors a craftsperson who has dedicated decades to perfecting a manual craft.

재개장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 재개장 (再開場), joining prefix 재- (再, 'again, re-') with 개장 (開場, 'opening a venue').
재개장.notes: Used for guesthouses, theatres, markets, and halls opening their doors anew.

재생.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 재생 (再生), combining 재 (再, 'again, a second time') and 생 (生, 'come alive, produce').
재생.notes: Means both ecological/material regeneration ('recycling, renewal') and audio/video playback ('bringing recorded sound back to life').

전화.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 전화 (電話), literally 'electric speech', coined in East Asia for the telephone.
전화.notes: Combines into 전화기 ('telephone set') and 전화번호 ('phone number').

절연.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 절연 (絶緣), from 절 (絶, 'sever, cut off') and 연 (緣, 'tie, connection, edge').
절연.notes: Means severing personal ties in literary prose, and blocking electrical current ('insulation') in engineering.

점검.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 점검 (點檢), from 점 (點, 'dot, itemize, check off') and 검 (檢, 'inspect, verify').
점검.notes: Originally meant checking off items one dot at a time on an inventory roll.

정오.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 정오 (正午), from 정 (正, 'exact, upright') and 오 (午, 'the Horse hour', 11 a.m.–1 p.m., whose midpoint is twelve noon).
정오.notes: Explains 오전 (午前, 'before noon / a.m.') and 오후 (午後, 'after noon / p.m.') as well.

제목.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 제목 (題目), combining 제 (題, 'forehead, heading, inscription') and 목 (目, 'eye, item, heading').
제목.notes: Standard word for the title of a piece of sheet music, book, or article.

제빵사.etymology: A compound of Sino-Korean 제 (製) 'make', 빵 'bread' and Sino-Korean 사 (師) 'master, specialist'.

조성.etymology: Sino-Korean musical compound 조성 (調性), from 조 (調, 'melody, tune, key') and 성 (性, 'nature, quality').
조성.notes: Distinguishes musical tonality/key from unrelated homographs of 조.

조율.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 조율 (調律), combining 조 (調, 'adjust, harmonize') and 율 (律, 'musical pitch, standard').
조율.notes: Used both literally for tuning stringed instruments and figuratively for coordinating plans.

조합.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 조합 (組合), from 조 (組, 'braid, group, pair') and 합 (合, 'join, unite').
조합.notes: Common in food talk for a winning flavour pairing (꿀조합, 좋은 조합).

죄송하다.etymology: Derived from Sino-Korean 죄송 (罪悚, literally 'guilty and fearful') combined with 하다.
죄송하다.notes: Standard polite expression for 'I am sorry' toward guests, strangers, and elders; casual speech prefers native 미안하다.

찻잔.etymology: Compound of Sino-Korean 차 (茶, 'tea') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 잔 (盞, 'cup').
찻잔.notes: Written with linking ㅅ because both nouns are established monosyllabic Sino-Korean roots acting like native compounds.

찻집.etymology: A compound of 차 'tea' and native 집 'house', joined by the linking ㅅ (사이시옷) written under 차.
찻집.notes: The same linking ㅅ appears in 찻잔 'teacup'.

창문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 창문 (窓門), joining 창 (窓, 'window') and 문 (門, 'door, opening').
창문.notes: Traditional Korean architecture built lattice windows that swing or slide like small doors, making 창문 completely natural.

천장.etymology: Sino-Korean 天障, literally the 'sky screen' above a room.

초인종.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 초인종 (招人鐘): 초 (招, 'summon, invite') + 인 (人, 'person') + 종 (鐘, 'bell').
초인종.notes: Literally 'a bell for calling someone'—the everyday Korean word for a doorbell or room buzzer.

축배.etymology: Sino-Korean 축배 (祝杯), from 축 (祝, 'celebrate, felicitate') + 배 (杯, 'cup, goblet').
축배.notes: Idiomatic in 축배를 들다 ('raise a celebratory glass / celebrate victory').

카페.notes: Modern Seoul neighbourhood word for coffeehouses and bakery cafés, largely superseding the mid-20th-century 다방 (茶房).

커피.etymology: Borrowed from English coffee, adapted to Korean phonology with ㅋ (k) for initial c and ㅍ (p) for English f (since Korean lacks a labiodental fricative).
커피.notes: Replaced the older late-19th-century phonetic transcription 가배 (珈琲) in modern Korean.

케이크.etymology: Borrowed from English cake, adding epenthetic 으 (-크) because Korean syllables do not end in an aspirated ㅋ release.
케이크.notes: Often shortened in casual speech to 케익, though 케이크 is the standard spelling.

택시.etymology: Borrowed from English taxi, preserving both syllables as 택 (taek) + 시 (si).
택시.notes: Pairs with the native verb 타다 ('택시를 타다', 'take a taxi') and 잡다 ('hail a taxi').

토요일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 토요일 (土曜日), combining 토 (土, 'earth / Saturn'), 요 (曜, 'celestial luminary'), and 일 (日, 'day').
토요일.notes: Part of the traditional East Asian seven-luminaries week cycle adopted into modern Korean calendar usage.

특급.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 특급 (特急), shortened from 특별 급행 (特別急行, 'special express') or 特級 ('special grade').
특급.notes: Widely used on express trains and courier vans (특급 배달, 'express delivery').

포장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 포장 (包裝), joining 포 (包, 'wrap, bundle') and 장 (裝, 'dress, pack, outfit').
포장.notes: Also used at Korean restaurants and bakeries in 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it to go').

폭우.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 폭우 (暴雨), from 폭 (暴, 'violent, sudden, fierce') and 우 (雨, 'rain').
폭우.notes: Shares 폭 (暴, 'fierce') with 폭풍 (暴風, 'storm') and 폭설 (暴雪, 'heavy snowfall').

폭풍.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 폭풍 (暴風), combining 폭 (暴, 'fierce, violent') and 풍 (風, 'wind').
폭풍.notes: Pronounced [폭풍] with unreleased [ㄱ] before aspirated ㅍ.

피아노.etymology: Borrowed from English/Italian piano (short for Italian pianoforte, 'soft-loud').
피아노.notes: Takes the native Korean verb 치다 ('피아노를 치다', 'to play the piano').

한밤중.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native intensifying prefix 한- ('dead centre, peak'), native 밤 ('night'), and Sino-Korean 중 (中, 'middle').
한밤중.notes: Parallel to 한낮 ('high noon') and 한겨울 ('midwinter').

할아버지.etymology: Native Korean kinship compound from 한-/할- ('great, big', from 하다 'to be great/many' in Middle Korean) + 아버지 ('father').

햇살.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound joining 해 ('sun') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 살 ('rays, arrows, spokes').
햇살.notes: Evokes individual warm beams of sunlight streaming through a courtyard or window.

행운.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 행운 (幸運), from 행 (幸, 'good fortune, blessing') and 운 (運, 'revolving fate, luck').
행운.notes: Commonly paired with native verb 빌다 in 행운을 빌어요 ('wishing you good luck').

호텔.etymology: Borrowed from English hotel (ultimately French hôtel).
호텔.notes: Contrasts in scale with smaller neighbourhood 게스트하우스 ('guesthouses') and traditional 한옥 숙소.

홍차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 홍차 (紅茶), literally 'red tea', from 홍 (紅, 'crimson, reddish') + 차 (茶, 'tea').
홍차.notes: East Asian languages name black tea after the warm reddish-amber colour of the brewed liquid rather than the dry leaves.

화살표.etymology: A compound of native Korean 화살 'arrow' and Sino-Korean 표 (標) 'mark, symbol'.
화살표.notes: The arrow drawn on signs, maps and plans.

화음.etymology: Sino-Korean 화음 (和音), compounding 화 (和, 'harmonize, blend') + 음 (音, 'sound, tone').
화음.notes: Standard musical term for two or more notes sounding simultaneously in harmony.

황금빛.etymology: Hybrid compound uniting Sino-Korean 황금 (黃金, 'yellow gold') with native Korean 빛 ('light, gleam, colour').
황금빛.notes: Korean productively attaches native 빛 to nouns to describe warm luminous hues (보랏빛, 은빛, 황금빛).

흑백.notes: Used for old photos and films, and figuratively for right and wrong.
